Homo sapiens — Influenced by Enlightenment ideals, the Americas and Europe experienced a period of political revolutions known as the Age of Revolution.
Homo sapiens — The Napoleonic Wars raged through Europe in the early 1800s, Spain lost most of its colonies in the New World, while Europeans continued expansion into Africa – where European control went from 10% to almost 90% in less than 50 years – and Oceania.
Homo sapiens — In the 19th century, the British Empire expanded to become the world's largest empire.
Homo sapiens — A tenuous balance of power among European nations collapsed in 1914 with the outbreak of the First World War, one of the deadliest conflicts in history.
Homo sapiens — In the 1930s, a worldwide economic crisis led to the rise of authoritarian regimes and a Second World War, involving almost all of the world's countries.
Homo sapiens — The war's destruction led to the collapse of most global empires, leading to widespread decolonization.
Homo sapiens — Following the conclusion of the Second World War in 1945, the United States and the Soviet Union emerged as the remaining global superpowers.
Homo sapiens — This led to a Cold War that saw a struggle for global influence, including a nuclear arms race and a space race, ending in the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Homo sapiens — The current Information Age, spurred by the development of the Internet and artificial intelligence systems, sees the world becoming increasingly globalized and interconnected.
Homo sapiens — Early human settlements were dependent on proximity to water and – depending on the lifestyle – other natural resources used for subsistence, such as populations of animal prey for hunting and arable land for growing crops and grazing livestock.
Homo sapiens — Modern humans, however, have a great capacity for altering their habitats by means of technology, irrigation, urban planning, construction, deforestation and desertification.
Homo sapiens — Human settlements continue to be vulnerable to natural disasters, especially those placed in hazardous locations and with low quality of construction.
Homo sapiens — Grouping and deliberate habitat alteration is often done with the goals of providing protection, accumulating comforts or material wealth, expanding the available food, improving aesthetics, increasing knowledge or enhancing the exchange of resources.
Homo sapiens — Humans are one of the most adaptable species, despite having a low or narrow tolerance for many of the earth's extreme environments.
Homo sapiens — Currently the species is present in all eight biogeographical realms, although their presence in the Antarctic realm is very limited to research stations and annually there is a population decline in the winter months of this realm.
Homo sapiens — Humans established nation-states in the other seven realms, such as South Africa, India, Russia, Australia, Fiji, the United States, and Brazil (each located in a different biogeographical realm).
Homo sapiens — Within the last century, humans have also explored the deep sea and outer space.
Homo sapiens — Human habitation within these hostile environments is restrictive and expensive, typically limited in duration, and restricted to scientific, military, or industrial expeditions.
Homo sapiens — Humans have visited the Moon and made their presence known on other celestial bodies through human-made robotic spacecraft.
Homo sapiens — Since 2000, there has been continuous human presence in space through habitation on the International Space Station.
Homo sapiens — By using advanced tools and clothing, humans have been able to extend their tolerance to a wide variety of temperatures, humidities, and altitudes.
Homo sapiens — As a result, humans are a cosmopolitan species found in almost all regions of the world, including tropical rainforest, arid desert, extremely cold arctic regions, and heavily polluted cities; in comparison, most other species are confined to a few geographical areas by their limited adaptability.
Homo sapiens — The human population is not, however, uniformly distributed on the Earth's surface, because the population density varies from one region to another, and large stretches of surface are almost completely uninhabited, like Antarctica and vast swathes of the ocean.
Homo sapiens — Most humans (61%) live in Asia; the remainder live in the Americas (14%), Africa (14%), Europe (11%), and Oceania (0.5%).
Homo sapiens — Estimates of the population at the time agriculture emerged in around 10,000 BC have ranged between 1 million and 15 million.
Homo sapiens — Around 50–60 million people lived in the combined eastern and western Roman Empire in the 4th century AD.
Homo sapiens — Bubonic plagues, first recorded in the 6th century AD, reduced the population by 50%, with the Black Death killing 75–200 million people in Eurasia and North Africa alone.
Homo sapiens — It has since then increased exponentially, reaching two billion in 1930 and three billion in 1960, four in 1975, five in 1987 and six billion in 1999.
Homo sapiens — It took over two million years of human prehistory and history for the human population to reach one billion and only 207 years more to grow to 7 billion.
Homo sapiens — The combined biomass of the carbon of all the humans on Earth in 2018 was estimated at 60 million tons, about 10 times larger than that of all non-domesticated mammals.
Homo sapiens — In 2018, 4.2 billion humans (55%) lived in urban areas, up from 751 million in 1950.
Homo sapiens — The most urbanized regions are Northern America (82%), Latin America (81%), Europe (74%) and Oceania (68%), with Africa and Asia having nearly 90% of the world's 3.4 billion rural population.
Homo sapiens — Problems for humans living in cities include various forms of pollution and crime, especially in inner city and suburban slums.
Homo sapiens — Most aspects of human physiology are closely homologous to corresponding aspects of animal physiology.
Homo sapiens — Humans have proportionately shorter palates and much smaller teeth than other primates.
Homo sapiens — Humans have characteristically crowded teeth, with gaps from lost teeth usually closing up quickly in young individuals.
Homo sapiens — Humans are gradually losing their third molars, with some individuals having them congenitally absent.
Homo sapiens — Humans share with chimpanzees a vestigial tail, appendix, flexible shoulder joints, grasping fingers and opposable thumbs.
Homo sapiens — Humans also have a more barrel-shaped chest in contrast to the funnel shape of other apes, an adaptation for bipedal respiration.
Homo sapiens — Apart from bipedalism and brain size, humans differ from chimpanzees mostly in smelling, hearing and digesting proteins.
Homo sapiens — While humans have a density of hair follicles comparable to other apes, it is predominantly vellus hair, most of which is so short and wispy as to be practically invisible.
Homo sapiens — Humans have about 2 million sweat glands spread over their entire bodies, many more than chimpanzees, whose sweat glands are scarce and are mainly located on the palm of the hand and on the soles of the feet.
Homo sapiens — It is estimated that the worldwide average height for an adult human male is about 171 cm (5 ft 7 in), while the worldwide average height for adult human females is about 159 cm (5 ft 3 in).
Homo sapiens — Shrinkage of stature may begin in middle age in some individuals but tends to be typical in the extremely aged.
Homo sapiens — Throughout history, human populations have universally become taller, probably as a consequence of better nutrition, healthcare, and living conditions.
Homo sapiens — The average mass of an adult human is 59 kg (130 lb) for females and 77 kg (170 lb) for males.
Homo sapiens — Like many other conditions, body weight and body type are influenced by both genetic susceptibility and environment and varies greatly among individuals.
Homo sapiens — Humans are also among the best long-distance runners in the animal kingdom, but slower over short distances.
Homo sapiens — Humans' thinner body hair and more productive sweat glands help avoid heat exhaustion while running for long distances.
Homo sapiens — Compared to other apes, the human heart produces greater stroke volume and cardiac output and the aorta is proportionately larger.
Homo sapiens — Humans are, like most animals, plants, and fungi, a eukaryotic, and like most animals a diploid species.
Homo sapiens — Each somatic cell has two sets of 23 chromosomes, each set received from one parent; gametes have only one set of chromosomes, which is a mixture of the two parental sets.
Homo sapiens — Among the 23 pairs of chromosomes, there are 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.
Homo sapiens — Like other mammals, humans have an XY sex-determination system, so that females have the sex chromosomes XX and males have XY.
Homo sapiens — Genes and environment influence human biological variation in visible characteristics, physiology, disease susceptibility and mental abilities.
Homo sapiens — The exact influence of genes and environment on certain traits is not well understood.
Homo sapiens — While no humans – not even monozygotic twins – are genetically identical, two humans on average will have a genetic similarity of 99.5%-99.9%.
Homo sapiens — This small variation in human DNA compared to many other species suggests a population bottleneck during the Late Pleistocene (around 100,000 years ago), in which the human population was reduced to a small number of breeding pairs.
Homo sapiens — The forces of natural selection have continued to operate on human populations, with evidence that certain regions of the genome display directional selection in the past 15,000 years.
Homo sapiens — The human genome was first sequenced in 2001 and by 2020 hundreds of thousands of genomes had been sequenced.
Homo sapiens — In 2012 the International HapMap Project had compared the genomes of 1,184 individuals from 11 populations and identified 1.6 million single nucleotide polymorphisms.
Homo sapiens — While many of the common variants found in populations outside of Africa are also found on the African continent, there are still large numbers that are private to these regions, especially Oceania and the Americas.
Homo sapiens — By comparing mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited only from the mother, geneticists have concluded that the last female common ancestor whose genetic marker is found in all modern humans, the so-called mitochondrial Eve, must have lived around 90,000 to 200,000 years ago.
Homo sapiens — Most human reproduction takes place by internal fertilization via sexual intercourse, but can also occur through assisted reproductive technology procedures.
Homo sapiens — The average gestation period is 38 weeks, but a normal pregnancy can vary by up to 37 days.
Homo sapiens — Embryonic development in the human covers the first eight weeks of development; at the beginning of the ninth week the embryo is termed a fetus.
Homo sapiens — Humans are able to induce early labor or perform a caesarean section if the child needs to be born earlier for medical reasons.
Homo sapiens — In developed countries, infants are typically 3–4 kg (7–9 lb) in weight and 47–53 cm (19–21 in) in height at birth.
Homo sapiens — However, low birth weight is common in developing countries, and contributes to the high levels of infant mortality in these regions.
Homo sapiens — Compared with other species, human childbirth is dangerous, with a much higher risk of complications and death.
Homo sapiens — The size of the fetus's head is more closely matched to the pelvis than in other primates.
Homo sapiens — The reason for this is not completely understood, but it contributes to a painful labor that can last 24 hours or more.
Homo sapiens — The chances of a successful labor increased significantly during the 20th century in wealthier countries with the advent of new medical technologies.
Homo sapiens — In contrast, pregnancy and natural childbirth remain hazardous ordeals in developing regions of the world, with maternal death rates approximately 100 times greater than in developed countries.
Homo sapiens — Both the mother and the father provide care for human offspring, in contrast to other primates, where parental care is mostly done by the mother.
Homo sapiens — Helpless at birth, humans continue to grow for some years, typically reaching sexual maturity at 15 to 17 years of age.
Homo sapiens — The human life span has been split into various stages ranging from three to twelve.
Homo sapiens — The lengths of these stages have varied across cultures and time periods but is typified by an unusually rapid growth spurt during adolescence.
Homo sapiens — It has been proposed that menopause increases a woman's overall reproductive success by allowing her to invest more time and resources in her existing offspring, and in turn their children (the grandmother hypothesis), rather than by continuing to bear children into old age.
Homo sapiens — The life span of an individual depends on two major factors, genetics and lifestyle choices.
Homo sapiens — For various reasons, including biological/genetic causes, women live on average about four years longer than men.
Homo sapiens — As of 2018, the global average life expectancy at birth of a girl is estimated to be 74.9 years compared to 70.4 for a boy.
Homo sapiens — There are significant geographical variations in human life expectancy, mostly correlated with economic development – for example, life expectancy at birth in Hong Kong is 87.6 years for girls and 81.8 for boys, while in the Central African Republic, it is 55.0 years for girls and 50.6 for boys.
Homo sapiens — While one in five Europeans is 60 years of age or older, only one in twenty Africans is 60 years of age or older.
Homo sapiens — In 2012, the United Nations estimated that there were 316,600 living centenarians (humans of age 100 or older) worldwide.
Homo sapiens — Humans are omnivorous, capable of consuming a wide variety of plant and animal material.
Homo sapiens — Human groups have adopted a range of diets from purely vegan to primarily carnivorous.
Homo sapiens — In some cases, dietary restrictions in humans can lead to deficiency diseases; however, stable human groups have adapted to many dietary patterns through both genetic specialization and cultural conventions to use nutritionally balanced food sources.
Homo sapiens — The human diet is prominently reflected in human culture and has led to the development of food science.
Homo sapiens — Until the development of agriculture, Homo sapiens employed a hunter-gatherer method as their sole means of food collection.
Homo sapiens — This involved combining stationary food sources (such as fruits, grains, tubers, and mushrooms, insect larvae and aquatic mollusks) with wild game, which must be hunted and captured in order to be consumed.
Homo sapiens — It has been proposed that humans have used fire to prepare and cook food since the time of Homo erectus.
Homo sapiens — Human domestication of wild plants began about 11,700 years ago, leading to the development of agriculture, a gradual process called the Neolithic Revolution.
Homo sapiens — These dietary changes may also have altered human biology; the spread of dairy farming provided a new and rich source of food, leading to the evolution of the ability to digest lactose in some adults.
Homo sapiens — The types of food consumed, and how they are prepared, have varied widely by time, location, and culture.
Homo sapiens — In general, humans can survive for up to eight weeks without food, depending on stored body fat.
Homo sapiens — Survival without water is usually limited to three or four days, with a maximum of one week.
Homo sapiens — In 2020, it was estimated 9 million humans die every year from causes directly or indirectly related to starvation.
Homo sapiens — Childhood malnutrition is also common and contributes to the global burden of disease.
Homo sapiens — However, global food distribution is not even, and obesity among some human populations has increased rapidly, leading to health complications and increased mortality in some developed and a few developing countries.
Homo sapiens — Worldwide, over one billion people are obese, while in the United States 35% of people are obese, leading to this being described as an "obesity epidemic." Obesity is caused by consuming more calories than are expended, so excessive weight gain is usually caused by an energy-dense diet.
Homo sapiens — Food consumption is the first step of the digestive process, in which humans ultimately expel feces ranging in frequency from multiple times per day to multiple times per week.
Homo sapiens — === Biological variation === There is biological variation in the human species – with traits such as blood type, genetic diseases, cranial features, facial features, organ systems, eye color, hair color and texture, height and build, and skin color varying across the globe.
Homo sapiens — The typical height of an adult human is between 1.4 and 1.9 m (4 ft 7 in and 6 ft 3 in), although this varies significantly depending on sex, ethnic origin, and family bloodlines.
Homo sapiens — Body size is partly determined by genes and is also significantly influenced by environmental factors such as diet, exercise, and sleep patterns.
Homo sapiens — There is evidence that populations have adapted genetically to various external factors.
Homo sapiens — The genes that allow adult humans to digest lactose are present in high frequencies in populations that have long histories of cattle domestication and are more dependent on cow milk.
Homo sapiens — Sickle cell anemia, which may provide increased resistance to malaria, is frequent in populations where malaria is endemic.
Homo sapiens — Populations that have for a very long time inhabited specific climates tend to have developed specific phenotypes that are beneficial for those environments – short stature and stocky build in cold regions, tall and lanky in hot regions, and with high lung capacities or other adaptations at high altitudes.
Homo sapiens — Some populations have evolved highly unique adaptations to very specific environmental conditions, such as those advantageous to ocean-dwelling lifestyles and freediving in the Bajau.
Homo sapiens — Human hair ranges in color from red to blond to brown to black, which is the most frequent.
Homo sapiens — Hair color depends on the amount of melanin, with concentrations fading with increased age, leading to grey or even white hair.
Homo sapiens — Skin color can range from darkest brown to lightest peach, or even nearly white or colorless in cases of albinism.
Homo sapiens — It tends to vary clinally and generally correlates with the level of ultraviolet radiation in a particular geographic area, with darker skin mostly around the equator.
Homo sapiens — Skin darkening may have evolved as protection against ultraviolet solar radiation.
Homo sapiens — Light skin pigmentation protects against depletion of vitamin D, which requires sunlight to make.
Homo sapiens — Human skin also has a capacity to darken (tan) in response to exposure to ultraviolet radiation.
Homo sapiens — There is relatively little variation between human geographical populations, and most of the variation that occurs is at the individual level.
Homo sapiens — Much of human variation is continuous, often with no clear points of demarcation.
Homo sapiens — Genetic data shows that no matter how population groups are defined, two people from the same population group are almost as different from each other as two people from any two different population groups.
Homo sapiens — Dark-skinned populations that are found in Africa, Australia, and South Asia are not closely related to each other.
Homo sapiens — Genetic research has demonstrated that human populations native to the African continent are the most genetically diverse and genetic diversity decreases with migratory distance from Africa, possibly the result of bottlenecks during human migration.
Homo sapiens — These non-African populations acquired new genetic inputs from local admixture with archaic populations and have much greater variation from Neanderthals and Denisovans than is found in Africa, though Neanderthal admixture into African populations may be underestimated.
Homo sapiens — Furthermore, recent studies have found that populations in sub-Saharan Africa, and particularly West Africa, have ancestral genetic variation which predates modern humans and has been lost in most non-African populations.
Homo sapiens — Some of this ancestry is thought to originate from admixture with an unknown archaic hominin that diverged before the split of Neanderthals and modern humans.
Homo sapiens — Humans are a gonochoric species, meaning they are divided into male and female sexes.
Homo sapiens — While the nucleotide genetic variation of individuals of the same sex across global populations is no greater than 0.1%–0.5%, the genetic difference between males and females is between 1% and 2%.
Homo sapiens — On average, men have about 40–50% more upper-body strength and 20–30% more lower-body strength than women at the same weight, due to higher amounts of muscle and larger muscle fibers.
Homo sapiens — Women have lighter skin than men of the same population; this has been explained by a higher need for vitamin D in females during pregnancy and lactation.
Homo sapiens — As there are chromosomal differences between females and males, some X and Y chromosome-related conditions and disorders only affect either men or women.
Homo sapiens — After allowing for body weight and volume, the male voice is usually an octave deeper than the female voice.
Homo sapiens — The human brain, the focal point of the central nervous system in humans, controls the peripheral nervous system.
Homo sapiens — In addition to controlling "lower", involuntary, or primarily autonomic activities such as respiration and digestion, it is also the locus of "higher" order functioning such as thought, reasoning, and abstraction.
Homo sapiens — These cognitive processes constitute the mind, and, along with their behavioral consequences, are studied in the field of psychology.
Homo sapiens — Humans have a larger and more developed prefrontal cortex than other primates, the region of the brain associated with higher cognition.
Homo sapiens — This has led humans to proclaim themselves to be more intelligent than any other known species.
Homo sapiens — Objectively defining intelligence is difficult, with other animals adapting senses and excelling in areas that humans are unable to.
Homo sapiens — There are some traits that, although not strictly unique, do set humans apart from other animals.
Homo sapiens — Humans may be the only animals who have episodic memory and who can engage in "mental time travel".
Homo sapiens — Even compared with other social animals, humans have an unusually high degree of flexibility in their facial expressions.
Homo sapiens — Humans are one of the few animals able to self-recognize in mirror tests and there is also debate over to what extent humans are the only animals with a theory of mind.
Homo sapiens — The average sleep requirement is between seven and nine hours per day for an adult and nine to ten hours per day for a child; elderly people usually sleep for six to seven hours.
Homo sapiens — Having less sleep than this is common among humans, even though sleep deprivation can have negative health effects.
Homo sapiens — A sustained restriction of adult sleep to four hours per day has been shown to correlate with changes in physiology and mental state, including reduced memory, fatigue, aggression, and bodily discomfort.
Homo sapiens — Dreaming is stimulated by the pons and mostly occurs during the REM phase of sleep.
Homo sapiens — Dreamers are more likely to remember the dream if awakened during the REM phase.
Homo sapiens — The events in dreams are generally outside the control of the dreamer, with the exception of lucid dreaming, where the dreamer is self-aware.
Homo sapiens — Dreams can at times make a creative thought occur or give a sense of inspiration.
Homo sapiens — Human consciousness, at its simplest, is sentience or awareness of internal or external existence.
Homo sapiens — Despite centuries of analyses, definitions, explanations and debates by philosophers and scientists, the underlying nature of consciousness remains enigmatic and poorly understood, being "at once the most familiar and most mysterious aspect of our lives".
Homo sapiens — Opinions differ about what exactly needs to be studied and explained as consciousness.
Homo sapiens — Some philosophers divide consciousness into phenomenal consciousness, which is sensory experience itself, and access consciousness, which can be used for reasoning or directly controlling actions.
Homo sapiens — It is sometimes synonymous with 'the mind', and at other times, an aspect of it.
Homo sapiens — Historically it is associated with introspection, private thought, imagination and volition.
Homo sapiens — It now often includes some kind of experience, cognition, feeling or perception.
Homo sapiens — There might be different levels or orders of consciousness, or different kinds of consciousness, or just one kind with different features.
Homo sapiens — The process of acquiring knowledge and understanding through thought, experience, and the senses is known as cognition.
Homo sapiens — The human brain perceives the external world through the senses, and each individual human is influenced greatly by his or her experiences, leading to subjective views of existence and the passage of time.
Homo sapiens — Cognitive psychology studies cognition, the mental processes underlying behavior.
Homo sapiens — Largely focusing on the development of the human mind through the life span, developmental psychology seeks to understand how people come to perceive, understand, and act within the world and how these processes change as they age.
Homo sapiens — This may focus on intellectual, cognitive, neural, social, or moral development.
Homo sapiens — Psychologists have developed intelligence tests and the concept of intelligence quotient in order to assess the relative intelligence of human beings and study its distribution among population.
Homo sapiens — From a psychological perspective, Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a well-established theory that can be defined as the process of satisfying certain needs in ascending order of complexity.
Homo sapiens — From a more general, philosophical perspective, human motivation can be defined as a commitment to, or withdrawal from, various goals requiring the application of human ability.
Homo sapiens — Furthermore, incentive and preference are both factors, as are any perceived links between incentives and preferences.
Homo sapiens — Ideally, both motivation and volition ensure the selection, striving for, and realization of goals in an optimal manner, a function beginning in childhood and continuing throughout a lifetime in a process known as socialization.
Homo sapiens — Emotions are biological states associated with the nervous system brought on by neurophysiological changes variously associated with thoughts, feelings, behavioral responses, and a degree of pleasure or displeasure.
Homo sapiens — They are often intertwined with mood, temperament, personality, disposition, creativity, and motivation.
Homo sapiens — Emotion has a significant influence on human behavior and their ability to learn.
Homo sapiens — Acting on extreme or uncontrolled emotions can lead to social disorder and crime, with studies showing criminals may have a lower emotional intelligence than normal.
Homo sapiens — Emotional experiences perceived as pleasant, such as joy, interest or contentment, contrast with those perceived as unpleasant, like anxiety, sadness, anger, and despair.
Homo sapiens — Some define it as experiencing the feeling of positive emotional affects, while avoiding the negative ones.
Homo sapiens — Recent research suggests that being happy might involve experiencing some negative emotions when humans feel they are warranted.
Homo sapiens — For humans, sexuality involves biological, erotic, physical, emotional, social, or spiritual feelings and behaviors.
Homo sapiens — Because it is a broad term, which has varied with historical contexts over time, it lacks a precise definition.
Homo sapiens — The biological and physical aspects of sexuality largely concern the human reproductive functions, including the human sexual response cycle.
Homo sapiens — Sexuality also affects and is affected by cultural, political, legal, philosophical, moral, ethical, and religious aspects of life.
Homo sapiens — Sexual desire, or libido, is a basic mental state present at the beginning of sexual behavior.
Homo sapiens — Humans can fall anywhere along a continuous scale of sexual orientation, although most humans are heterosexual.
Homo sapiens — While homosexual behavior occurs in some other animals, only humans and domestic sheep have so far been found to exhibit exclusive preference for same-sex relationships.
Homo sapiens — Most evidence supports nonsocial, biological causes of sexual orientation, as cultures that are very tolerant of homosexuality do not have significantly higher rates of it.
Homo sapiens — Research in neuroscience and genetics suggests that other aspects of human sexuality are biologically influenced as well.
Homo sapiens — Love most commonly refers to a feeling of strong attraction or emotional attachment.
Homo sapiens — It can be impersonal (the love of an object, ideal, or strong political or spiritual connection) or interpersonal (love between humans).
Homo sapiens — When in love dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and other chemicals stimulate the brain's pleasure center, leading to side effects such as increased heart rate, loss of appetite and sleep, and an intense feeling of excitement.
Homo sapiens — Humanity's unprecedented set of intellectual skills were a key factor in the species' eventual technological advancement and concomitant domination of the biosphere.
Homo sapiens — Disregarding extinct hominids, humans are the only animals known to teach generalizable information, innately deploy recursive embedding to generate and communicate complex concepts, engage in the "folk physics" required for competent tool design, or cook food in the wild.
Homo sapiens — Teaching and learning preserves the cultural and ethnographic identity of human societies.
Homo sapiens — Other traits and behaviors that are mostly unique to humans include starting fires, phoneme structuring and vocal learning.
Homo sapiens — While many species communicate, language is unique to humans, a defining feature of humanity, and a cultural universal.
Homo sapiens — Unlike the limited systems of other animals, human language is open – an infinite number of meanings can be produced by combining a limited number of symbols.
Homo sapiens — Human language also has the capacity of displacement, using words to represent things and happenings that are not presently or locally occurring but reside in the shared imagination of interlocutors.
Homo sapiens — Language differs from other forms of communication in that it is modality independent; the same meanings can be conveyed through different media, audibly in speech, visually by sign language or writing, and through tactile media such as braille.
Homo sapiens — Language is central to the communication between humans, and to the sense of identity that unites nations, cultures and ethnic groups.
Homo sapiens — There are approximately six thousand different languages currently in use, including sign languages, and many thousands more that are extinct.
Homo sapiens — === The arts === Human arts can take many forms including visual, literary, and performing.
Homo sapiens — Visual art can range from paintings and sculptures to film, fashion design, and architecture.
Homo sapiens — Other entities that have been described as having artistic qualities include food preparation, video games, and medicine.
Homo sapiens — As well as providing entertainment and transferring knowledge, the arts are also used for political purposes.
Homo sapiens — Art is a defining characteristic of humans and there is evidence for a relationship between creativity and language.
Homo sapiens — The earliest evidence of art was shell engravings made by Homo erectus 300,000 years before modern humans evolved.
Homo sapiens — Art attributed to H. sapiens existed at least 75,000 years ago, with jewellery and drawings found in caves in South Africa.
Homo sapiens — These include allowing them to better problem solve issues, providing a means to control or influence other humans, encouraging cooperation and contribution within a society or increasing the chance of attracting a potential mate.
Homo sapiens — The use of imagination developed through art, combined with logic may have given early humans an evolutionary advantage.
Homo sapiens — Evidence of humans engaging in musical activities predates cave art and so far music has been practiced by virtually all known human cultures.
Homo sapiens — There exists a wide variety of music genres and ethnic musics; with humans' musical abilities being related to other abilities, including complex social human behaviours.
Homo sapiens — It has been shown that human brains respond to music by becoming synchronized with the rhythm and beat, a process called entrainment.
Homo sapiens — Dance is also a form of human expression found in all cultures and may have evolved as a way to help early humans communicate.
Homo sapiens — Listening to music and observing dance stimulates the orbitofrontal cortex and other pleasure sensing areas of the brain.
Homo sapiens — Unlike speaking, reading and writing does not come naturally to humans and must be taught.
Homo sapiens — Still, literature has been present before the invention of words and language, with 30,000-year-old paintings on walls inside some caves portraying a series of dramatic scenes.
Homo sapiens — One of the oldest surviving works of literature is the Epic of Gilgamesh, first engraved on ancient Babylonian tablets about 4,000 years ago.
Homo sapiens — Beyond simply passing down knowledge, the use and sharing of imaginative fiction through stories might have helped develop humans' capabilities for communication and increased the likelihood of securing a mate.
Homo sapiens — Storytelling may also be used as a way to provide the audience with moral lessons and encourage cooperation.
Homo sapiens — The use and manufacture of tools has been put forward as the ability that defines humans more than anything else and has historically been seen as an important evolutionary step.
Homo sapiens — The technology became much more sophisticated about 1.8 million years ago, with the controlled use of fire beginning around 1 million years ago.
Homo sapiens — The wheel and wheeled vehicles appeared simultaneously in several regions some time in the fourth millennium BC.
Homo sapiens — The development of more complex tools and technologies allowed land to be cultivated and animals to be domesticated, thus proving essential in the development of agriculture – what is known as the Neolithic Revolution.
Homo sapiens — China developed paper, the printing press, gunpowder, the compass and other important inventions.
Homo sapiens — The continued improvements in smelting allowed forging of copper, bronze, iron and eventually steel, which is used in railways, skyscrapers and many other products.
Homo sapiens — This coincided with the Industrial Revolution, where the invention of automated machines brought major changes to humans' lifestyles.
Homo sapiens — Modern technology is observed as progressing exponentially, with major innovations in the 20th century including: electricity, penicillin, semiconductors, internal combustion engines, the Internet, nitrogen fixing fertilizers, airplanes, computers, automobiles, contraceptive pills, nuclear fission, the green revolution, radio, scientific plant breeding, rockets, air conditioning, television and the assembly line.
Homo sapiens — Definitions of religion vary; according to one definition, a religion is a belief system concerning the supernatural, sacred or divine, and practices, values, institutions and rituals associated with such belief.
Homo sapiens — The evolution and the history of the first religions have become areas of active scientific investigation.
Homo sapiens — Credible evidence of religious behaviour dates to the Middle Paleolithic era (45–200 thousand years ago).
Homo sapiens — It may have evolved to play a role in helping enforce and encourage cooperation between humans.
Homo sapiens — Religion can include a belief in life after death, the origin of life, the nature of the universe (religious cosmology) and its ultimate fate (eschatology), and moral or ethical teachings.
Homo sapiens — Views on transcendence and immanence vary substantially; traditions variously espouse monism, deism, pantheism, and theism (including polytheism and monotheism).
Homo sapiens — Although measuring religiosity is difficult, a majority of humans profess some variety of religious or spiritual belief.
Homo sapiens — As of 2015, about 16%, or slightly under 1.2 billion humans, were irreligious, including those with no religious beliefs or no identity with any religion.
Homo sapiens — An aspect unique to humans is their ability to transmit knowledge from one generation to the next and to continually build on this information to develop tools, scientific laws and other advances to pass on further.
Homo sapiens — This accumulated knowledge can be tested to answer questions or make predictions about how the universe functions and has been very successful in advancing human ascendancy.
Homo sapiens — Aristotle has been described as the first scientist, and preceded the rise of scientific thought through the Hellenistic period.
Homo sapiens — Other early advances in science came from the Han dynasty in China and during the Islamic Golden Age.
Homo sapiens — The scientific revolution, near the end of the Renaissance, led to the emergence of modern science.
Homo sapiens — A chain of events and influences led to the development of the scientific method, a process of observation and experimentation that is used to differentiate science from pseudoscience.
Homo sapiens — An understanding of mathematics is unique to humans, although other species of animals have some numerical cognition.
Homo sapiens — All of science can be divided into three major branches, the formal sciences (e.g., logic and mathematics), which are concerned with formal systems, the applied sciences (e.g., engineering, medicine), which are focused on practical applications, and the empirical sciences, which are based on empirical observation and are in turn divided into natural sciences (e.g., physics, chemistry, biology) and social sciences (e.g., psychology, economics, sociology).
Homo sapiens — Philosophy is a field of study where humans seek to understand fundamental truths about themselves and the world in which they live.
Homo sapiens — Philosophical inquiry has been a major feature in the development of humans' intellectual history.
Homo sapiens — It has been described as the "no man's land" between definitive scientific knowledge and dogmatic religious teachings.
Homo sapiens — Major fields of philosophy include metaphysics, epistemology, logic, and axiology (which includes ethics and aesthetics).
Homo sapiens — Society is the system of organizations and institutions arising from interaction between humans.
Homo sapiens — They can be divided into different groups according to their income, wealth, power, reputation and other factors.
Homo sapiens — The structure of social stratification and the degree of social mobility differs, especially between modern and traditional societies.
Homo sapiens — The first form of human social organization is thought to have resembled hunter-gatherer band societies.
Homo sapiens — Human societies typically exhibit gender identities and gender roles that distinguish between masculine and feminine characteristics and prescribe the range of acceptable behaviours and attitudes for their members based on their sex.
Homo sapiens — In some other societies, non-binary is used as an umbrella term for a range of gender identities that are not solely male or female.
Homo sapiens — Gender roles are often associated with a division of norms, practices, dress, behavior, rights, duties, privileges, status, and power, with men enjoying more rights and privileges than women in most societies, both today and in the past.
Homo sapiens — As a social construct, gender roles are not fixed and vary historically within a society.
Homo sapiens — Early modern humans probably had a range of gender roles similar to that of modern cultures from at least the Upper Paleolithic, while the Neanderthals were less sexually dimorphic and there is evidence that the behavioural difference between males and females was minimal.
Homo sapiens — All human societies organize, recognize and classify types of social relationships based on relations between parents, children and other descendants (consanguinity), and relations through marriage (affinity).
Homo sapiens — There is also a third type applied to godparents or adoptive children (fictive).
Homo sapiens — In many societies, it is one of the most important social organizing principles and plays a role in transmitting status and inheritance.
Homo sapiens — All societies have rules of incest taboo, according to which marriage between certain kinds of kin relations is prohibited, and some also have rules of preferential marriage with certain kin relations.
Homo sapiens — Pair bonding is a ubiquitous feature of human sexual relationships, whether it is manifested as serial monogamy, polygyny, or polyandry.
Homo sapiens — Genetic evidence indicates that humans were predominantly polygynous for most of their existence as a species, but that this began to shift during the Neolithic, when monogamy started becoming widespread concomitantly with the transition from nomadic to sedentary societies.
Homo sapiens — Anatomical evidence in the form of second-to-fourth digit ratios, a biomarker for prenatal androgen effects, likewise indicates modern humans were polygynous during the Pleistocene.
Homo sapiens — Human ethnic groups are a social category that identifies together as a group based on shared attributes that distinguish them from other groups.
Homo sapiens — These can be a common set of traditions, ancestry, language, history, society, culture, nation, religion, or social treatment within their residing area.
Homo sapiens — Ethnicity is separate from the concept of race, which is based on physical characteristics, although both are socially constructed.
Homo sapiens — Assigning ethnicity to a certain population is complicated, as even within common ethnic designations there can be a diverse range of subgroups, and the makeup of these ethnic groups can change over time at both the collective and individual level.
Homo sapiens — Also, there is no generally accepted definition of what constitutes an ethnic group.
Homo sapiens — Ethnic groupings can play a powerful role in the social identity and solidarity of ethnopolitical units.
Homo sapiens — This has been closely tied to the rise of the nation state as the predominant form of political organization in the 19th and 20th centuries.
Homo sapiens — As farming populations gathered in larger and denser communities, interactions between these different groups increased.
Homo sapiens — Humans have evolved the ability to change affiliation with various social groups relatively easily, including previously strong political alliances, if doing so is seen as providing personal advantages.
Homo sapiens — This cognitive flexibility allows individual humans to change their political ideologies, with those with higher flexibility less likely to support authoritarian and nationalistic stances.
Homo sapiens — There have been many forms of government throughout human history, each having various means of obtaining power and the ability to exert diverse controls on the population.
Homo sapiens — Approximately 47% of humans live in some form of a democracy, 17% in a hybrid regime, and 37% in an authoritarian regime.
Homo sapiens — Many countries belong to international organizations and alliances; the largest of these is the United Nations, with 193 member states.
Homo sapiens — Trade, the voluntary exchange of goods and services, is seen as a characteristic that differentiates humans from other animals and has been cited as a practice that gave Homo sapiens a major advantage over other hominids.
Homo sapiens — Evidence suggests early H. sapiens made use of long-distance trade routes to exchange goods and ideas, leading to cultural explosions and providing additional food sources when hunting was sparse, while such trade networks did not exist for the now extinct Neanderthals.
Homo sapiens — The first truly international trade routes were around the spice trade through the Roman and medieval periods.
Homo sapiens — Early human economies were more likely to be based around gift giving instead of a bartering system.
Homo sapiens — Early money consisted of commodities; the oldest being in the form of cattle and the most widely used being cowrie shells.
Homo sapiens — Money has since evolved into governmental issued coins, paper and electronic money.
Homo sapiens — Human study of economics is a social science that looks at how societies distribute scarce resources among different people.
Homo sapiens — There are massive inequalities in the division of wealth among humans; the eight richest humans are worth the same monetary value as the poorest half of all the human population.
Homo sapiens — Humans commit violence on other humans at a rate comparable to other primates, but have an increased preference for killing adults, infanticide being more common among other primates.
Homo sapiens — Phylogenetic analysis predicts that 2% of early H. sapiens would be murdered, rising to 12% during the medieval period, before dropping to below 2% in modern times.
Homo sapiens — There is great variation in violence between human populations, with rates of homicide about 0.01% in societies that have legal systems and strong cultural attitudes against violence.
Homo sapiens — The willingness of humans to kill other members of their species en masse through organized conflict (i.e., war) has long been the subject of debate.
Homo sapiens — One school of thought holds that war evolved as a means to eliminate competitors, and has always been an innate human characteristic.
Homo sapiens — Another suggests that war is a relatively recent phenomenon and has appeared due to changing social conditions.
Homo sapiens — While not settled, current evidence indicates warlike predispositions only became common about 10,000 years ago, and in many places much more recently than that.
Homo sapiens — War has had a high cost on human life; it is estimated that during the 20th century, between 167 million and 188 million people died as a result of war.
Homo sapiens — War casualty data is less reliable for pre-medieval times, especially global figures.
Homo sapiens — But compared with any period over the past 600 years, the last 80 years (post 1946) has seen a very significant drop in global military and civilian death rates due to armed conflict.
Human brain — The human brain is the central organ of the nervous system, and with the spinal cord, comprises the central nervous system.
Human brain — The brain controls most of the activities of the body, processing, integrating, and coordinating the information it receives from the sensory nervous system.
Human brain — The brain integrates sensory information and coordinates instructions sent to the rest of the body.
Human brain — The cerebrum, the largest part of the human brain, consists of two cerebral hemispheres.
Human brain — Each hemisphere has an inner core composed of white matter, and an outer surface – the cerebral cortex – composed of grey matter.
Human brain — The neocortex is made up of six neuronal layers, while the allocortex has three or four.
Human brain — Each hemisphere is divided into four lobes – the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes.
Human brain — The frontal lobe is associated with executive functions including self-control, planning, reasoning, and abstract thought, while the occipital lobe is dedicated to vision.
Human brain — Within each lobe, cortical areas are associated with specific functions, such as the sensory, motor, and association regions.
Human brain — Although the left and right hemispheres are broadly similar in shape and function, some functions are associated with one side, such as language in the left and visual-spatial ability in the right.
Human brain — The hemispheres are connected by commissural nerve tracts, the largest being the corpus callosum.
Human brain — The cerebellum is connected to the brainstem by three pairs of nerve tracts called cerebellar peduncles.
Human brain — Within the cerebrum is the ventricular system, consisting of four interconnected ventricles in which cerebrospinal fluid is produced and circulated.
Human brain — Underneath the cerebral cortex are several structures, including the thalamus, the epithalamus, the pineal gland, the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland, and the subthalamus; the limbic structures, including the amygdalae and the hippocampi, the claustrum, the various nuclei of the basal ganglia, the basal forebrain structures, and three circumventricular organs.
Human brain — Brain structures that are not on the midplane exist in pairs; for example, there are two hippocampi and two amygdalae.
Human brain — There are more than 86 billion neurons in the brain, and a more or less equal number of other cells.
Human brain — Brain activity is made possible by the interconnections of neurons and their release of neurotransmitters in response to nerve impulses.
Human brain — Neurons connect to form neural pathways, neural circuits, and elaborate network systems.
Human brain — The brain is protected by the skull, suspended in cerebrospinal fluid, and isolated from the bloodstream by the blood–brain barrier.
Human brain — The brain is susceptible to degenerative disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, dementias including Alzheimer's disease, and multiple sclerosis.
Human brain — Psychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia and clinical depression, are thought to be associated with brain dysfunctions.
Human brain — The brain can also be the site of tumours, both benign and malignant; these mostly originate from other sites in the body.
Human brain — The study of the anatomy of the brain is neuroanatomy, while the study of its function is neuroscience.
Human brain — Specimens from other animals, which may be examined microscopically, have traditionally provided much information.
Human brain — Medical imaging technologies such as functional neuroimaging, and electroencephalography (EEG) recordings are important in studying the brain.
Human brain — The medical history of people with brain injury has provided insight into the function of each part of the brain.
Human brain — In culture, the philosophy of mind has for centuries attempted to address the question of the nature of consciousness and the mind–body problem.
Human brain — The pseudoscience of phrenology attempted to localise personality attributes to regions of the cortex in the 19th century.
Human brain — In science fiction, brain transplants are imagined in tales such as the 1942 Donovan's Brain.
Human brain — The adult human brain weighs on average about 1.2–1.4 kg (2.6–3.1 lb) which is about 2% of the total body weight, with a volume of around 1260 cm3 in men and 1130 cm3 in women.
Human brain — There is substantial individual variation, with the standard reference range for men being 1,180–1,620 g (2.60–3.57 lb) and for women 1,030–1,400 g (2.27–3.09 lb).
Human brain — The cerebrum, consisting of the cerebral hemispheres, forms the largest part of the brain and overlies the other brain structures.
Human brain — The outer region of the hemispheres, the cerebral cortex, is grey matter, consisting of cortical layers of neurons.
Human brain — Each hemisphere is divided into four main lobes – the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and occipital lobe.
Human brain — Three other lobes are included by some sources which are a central lobe, a limbic lobe, and an insular lobe.
Human brain — The central lobe comprises the precentral gyrus and the postcentral gyrus and is included since it forms a distinct functional role.
Human brain — The brainstem, resembling a stalk, attaches to and leaves the cerebrum at the start of the midbrain area.
Human brain — The cerebrum, brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord are covered by three membranes called meninges.
Human brain — The membranes are the tough dura mater; the middle arachnoid mater and the more delicate inner pia mater.
Human brain — Between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater is the subarachnoid space and subarachnoid cisterns, which contain the cerebrospinal fluid.
Human brain — The outermost membrane of the cerebral cortex is the basement membrane of the pia mater called the glia limitans and is an important part of the blood–brain barrier.
Human brain — In 2023 a fourth meningeal membrane has been proposed known as the subarachnoid lymphatic-like membrane.
Human brain — The living brain is very soft, having a gel-like consistency similar to soft tofu.
Human brain — The cortical layers of neurons constitute much of the cerebral grey matter, while the deeper subcortical regions of myelinated axons, make up the white matter.
Human brain — The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and is divided into nearly symmetrical left and right hemispheres by a deep groove, the longitudinal fissure.
Human brain — The hemispheres are connected by five commissures that span the longitudinal fissure, the largest of these is the corpus callosum.
Human brain — Each hemisphere is conventionally divided into four main lobes; the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and occipital lobe, named according to the skull bones that overlie them.
Human brain — Each lobe is associated with one or two specialised functions though there is some functional overlap between them.
Human brain — The surface of the brain is folded into ridges (gyri) and grooves (sulci), many of which are named, usually according to their position, such as the frontal gyrus of the frontal lobe or the central sulcus separating the central regions of the hemispheres.
Human brain — The outer part of the cerebrum is the cerebral cortex, made up of grey matter arranged in layers.
Human brain — It is 2 to 4 millimetres (0.079 to 0.157 in) thick, and deeply folded to give a convoluted appearance.
Human brain — The largest part of the cerebral cortex is the neocortex, which has six neuronal layers.
Human brain — The cortex is mapped by divisions into about fifty different functional areas known as Brodmann's areas.
Human brain — The cortex is divided into two main functional areas – a motor cortex and a sensory cortex.
Human brain — The primary motor cortex, which sends axons down to motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord, occupies the rear portion of the frontal lobe, directly in front of the somatosensory area.
Human brain — The primary sensory areas receive signals from the sensory nerves and tracts by way of relay nuclei in the thalamus.
Human brain — Primary sensory areas include the visual cortex of the occipital lobe, the auditory cortex in parts of the temporal lobe and insular cortex, and the somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe.
Human brain — These areas receive input from the sensory areas and lower parts of the brain and are involved in the complex cognitive processes of perception, thought, and decision-making.
Human brain — The main functions of the frontal lobe are to control attention, abstract thinking, behaviour, problem-solving tasks, and physical reactions and personality.
Human brain — The occipital lobe is the smallest lobe; its main functions are visual reception, visual-spatial processing, movement, and colour recognition.
Human brain — The temporal lobe controls auditory and visual memories, language, and some hearing and speech.
Human brain — The cerebrum contains the ventricles where the cerebrospinal fluid is produced and circulated.
Human brain — Below the corpus callosum is the septum pellucidum, a membrane that separates the lateral ventricles.
Human brain — Beneath the lateral ventricles is the thalamus and to the front and below is the hypothalamus.
Human brain — The basal ganglia, also called basal nuclei, are a set of structures deep within the hemispheres involved in behaviour and movement regulation.
Human brain — The largest component is the striatum, others are the globus pallidus, the substantia nigra and the subthalamic nucleus.
Human brain — The striatum is divided into a ventral striatum, and dorsal striatum, subdivisions that are based upon function and connections.
Human brain — The ventral striatum consists of the nucleus accumbens and the olfactory tubercle whereas the dorsal striatum consists of the caudate nucleus and the putamen.
Human brain — The putamen and the globus pallidus lie separated from the lateral ventricles and thalamus by the internal capsule, whereas the caudate nucleus stretches around and abuts the lateral ventricles on their outer sides.
Human brain — At the deepest part of the lateral sulcus between the insular cortex and the striatum is a thin neuronal sheet called the claustrum.
Human brain — These include the nucleus basalis, diagonal band of Broca, substantia innominata, and the medial septal nucleus.
Human brain — These structures are important in producing the neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, which is then distributed widely throughout the brain.
Human brain — The basal forebrain, in particular the nucleus basalis, is considered to be the major cholinergic output of the central nervous system to the striatum and neocortex.
Human brain — The cerebellum is divided into an anterior lobe, a posterior lobe, and the flocculonodular lobe.
Human brain — Compared to the cerebral cortex, the cerebellum has a much thinner outer cortex that is narrowly furrowed into numerous curved transverse fissures.
Human brain — Viewed from underneath between the two lobes is the third lobe the flocculonodular lobe.
Human brain — The cerebellum rests at the back of the cranial cavity, lying beneath the occipital lobes, and is separated from these by the cerebellar tentorium, a sheet of fibre.
Human brain — It is connected to the brainstem by three pairs of nerve tracts called cerebellar peduncles.
Human brain — The superior pair connects to the midbrain; the middle pair connects to the medulla, and the inferior pair connects to the pons.
Human brain — The cerebellum consists of an inner medulla of white matter and an outer cortex of richly folded grey matter.
Human brain — The cerebellum's anterior and posterior lobes appear to play a role in the coordination and smoothing of complex motor movements, and the flocculonodular lobe in the maintenance of balance although debate exists as to its cognitive, behavioural and motor functions.
Human brain — The brainstem lies beneath the cerebrum and consists of the midbrain, pons and medulla.
Human brain — It lies in the back part of the skull, resting on the part of the base known as the clivus, and ends at the foramen magnum, a large opening in the occipital bone.
Human brain — The brainstem continues below this as the spinal cord, protected by the vertebral column.
Human brain — The brainstem also contains many cranial nerve nuclei and nuclei of peripheral nerves, as well as nuclei involved in the regulation of many essential processes including breathing, control of eye movements and balance.
Human brain — The reticular formation, a network of nuclei of ill-defined formation, is present within and along the length of the brainstem.
Human brain — Many nerve tracts, which transmit information to and from the cerebral cortex to the rest of the body, pass through the brainstem.
Human brain — === Microanatomy === The human brain is primarily composed of neurons, glial cells, neural stem cells, and blood vessels.
Human brain — Types of neuron include interneurons, pyramidal cells including Betz cells, motor neurons (upper and lower motor neurons), and cerebellar Purkinje cells.
Human brain — The adult human brain is estimated to contain 86±8 billion neurons, with a roughly equal number (85±10 billion) of non-neuronal cells.
Human brain — Out of these neurons, 16 billion (19%) are located in the cerebral cortex, and 69 billion (80%) are in the cerebellum.
Human brain — Types of glial cell are astrocytes (including Bergmann glia), oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells (including tanycytes), radial glial cells, microglia, and a subtype of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
Human brain — The glia limitans of the cortex is made up of astrocyte endfeet processes that serve in part to contain the cells of the brain.
Human brain — Mast cells are white blood cells that interact in the neuroimmune system in the brain.
Human brain — Mast cells in the central nervous system are present in a number of structures including the meninges; they mediate neuroimmune responses in inflammatory conditions and help to maintain the blood–brain barrier, particularly in brain regions where the barrier is absent.
Human brain — Mast cells serve the same general functions in the body and central nervous system, such as effecting or regulating allergic responses, innate and adaptive immunity, autoimmunity, and inflammation.
Human brain — Mast cells serve as the main effector cell through which pathogens can affect the biochemical signaling that takes place between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system.
Human brain — In all neurons, ELAVL3 is expressed, and in pyramidal cells, NRGN and REEP2 are also expressed.
Human brain — GAD1 – essential for the biosynthesis of the neurotransmitter GABA – is expressed in interneurons.
Human brain — Proteins expressed in glial cells include astrocyte markers GFAP and S100B whereas myelin basic protein and the transcription factor OLIG2 are expressed in oligodendrocytes.
Human brain — Cerebrospinal fluid is a clear, colourless transcellular fluid that circulates around the brain in the subarachnoid space, in the ventricular system, and in the central canal of the spinal cord.
Human brain — It also fills some gaps in the subarachnoid space, known as subarachnoid cisterns.
Human brain — The four ventricles, two lateral, a third, and a fourth ventricle, all contain a choroid plexus that produces cerebrospinal fluid.
Human brain — The third ventricle lies in the midline and is connected to the lateral ventricles.
Human brain — A single duct, the cerebral aqueduct between the pons and the cerebellum, connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle.
Human brain — Three separate openings, the middle and two lateral apertures, drain the cerebrospinal fluid from the fourth ventricle to the cisterna magna, one of the major cisterns.
Human brain — From here, cerebrospinal fluid circulates around the brain and spinal cord in the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and pia mater.
Human brain — At any one time, there is about 150mL of cerebrospinal fluid – most within the subarachnoid space.
Human brain — It is constantly being regenerated and absorbed, and is replaced about once every 5–6 hours.
Human brain — A glymphatic system has been described as the lymphatic drainage system of the brain.
Human brain — The brain-wide glymphatic pathway includes drainage routes from the cerebrospinal fluid, and from the meningeal lymphatic vessels that are associated with the dural sinuses, and run alongside the cerebral blood vessels.
Human brain — The internal carotid arteries supply oxygenated blood to the front of the brain and the vertebral arteries supply blood to the back of the brain.
Human brain — These two circulations join in the circle of Willis, a ring of connected arteries that lies in the interpeduncular cistern between the midbrain and pons.
Human brain — They enter the cranium through the carotid canal, travel through the cavernous sinus and enter the subarachnoid space.
Human brain — They then enter the circle of Willis, with two branches, the anterior cerebral arteries emerging.
Human brain — These branches travel forward and then upward along the longitudinal fissure, and supply the front and midline parts of the brain.
Human brain — One or more small anterior communicating arteries join the two anterior cerebral arteries shortly after they emerge as branches.
Human brain — They travel sideways along the sphenoid bone of the eye socket, then upwards through the insula cortex, where final branches arise.
Human brain — The vertebral arteries emerge as branches of the left and right subclavian arteries.
Human brain — They travel upward through transverse foramina which are spaces in the cervical vertebrae.
Human brain — Each side enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum along the corresponding side of the medulla.
Human brain — The vertebral arteries join in front of the middle part of the medulla to form the larger basilar artery, which sends multiple branches to supply the medulla and pons, and the two other anterior and superior cerebellar branches.
Human brain — These travel outwards, around the superior cerebellar peduncles, and along the top of the cerebellar tentorium, where it sends branches to supply the temporal and occipital lobes.
Human brain — Each posterior cerebral artery sends a small posterior communicating artery to join with the internal carotid arteries.
Human brain — ==== Blood drainage ==== Cerebral veins drain deoxygenated blood from the brain.
Human brain — The brain has two main networks of veins: an exterior or superficial network, on the surface of the cerebrum that has three branches, and an interior network.
Human brain — The veins of the brain drain into larger cavities of the dural venous sinuses usually situated between the dura mater and the covering of the skull.
Human brain — Blood from the medulla and pons of the brainstem have a variable pattern of drainage, either into the spinal veins or into adjacent cerebral veins.
Human brain — The blood in the deep part of the brain drains, through a venous plexus into the cavernous sinus at the front, and the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses at the sides, and the inferior sagittal sinus at the back.
Human brain — Blood drains from the outer brain into the large superior sagittal sinus, which rests in the midline on top of the brain.
Human brain — Blood from here joins with blood from the straight sinus at the confluence of sinuses.
Human brain — These then drain into the sigmoid sinuses, which receive blood from the cavernous sinus and superior and inferior petrosal sinuses.
Human brain — ==== The blood–brain barrier ==== The larger arteries throughout the brain supply blood to smaller capillaries.
Human brain — These smallest of blood vessels in the brain, are lined with cells joined by tight junctions and so fluids do not seep in or leak out to the same degree as they do in other capillaries; this creates the blood–brain barrier.
Human brain — The barrier is less permeable to larger molecules, but is still permeable to water, carbon dioxide, oxygen, and most fat-soluble substances (including anaesthetics and alcohol).
Human brain — The blood-brain barrier is not present in the circumventricular organs—which are structures in the brain that may need to respond to changes in body fluids—such as the pineal gland, area postrema, and some areas of the hypothalamus.
Human brain — There is a similar blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier, which serves the same purpose as the blood–brain barrier, but facilitates the transport of different substances into the brain due to the distinct structural characteristics between the two barrier systems.
Human brain — At the beginning of the third week of development, the embryonic ectoderm forms a thickened strip called the neural plate.
Human brain — By the fourth week of development the neural plate has widened to give a broad cephalic end, a less broad middle part and a narrow caudal end.
Human brain — These swellings are known as the primary brain vesicles and represent the beginnings of the forebrain (prosencephalon), midbrain (mesencephalon), and hindbrain (rhombencephalon).
Human brain — Neural crest cells (derived from the ectoderm) populate the lateral edges of the plate at the neural folds.
Human brain — In the fourth week—during the neurulation stage—the neural folds close to form the neural tube, bringing together the neural crest cells at the neural crest.
Human brain — The neural crest runs the length of the tube with cranial neural crest cells at the cephalic end and caudal neural crest cells at the tail.
Human brain — Cells detach from the crest and migrate in a craniocaudal (head to tail) wave inside the tube.
Human brain — Cells at the cephalic end give rise to the brain, and cells at the caudal end give rise to the spinal cord.
Human brain — The tube flexes as it grows, forming the crescent-shaped cerebral hemispheres at the head.
Human brain — Early in the fourth week, the cephalic part bends sharply forward in a cephalic flexure.
Human brain — This flexed part becomes the forebrain (prosencephalon); the adjoining curving part becomes the midbrain (mesencephalon) and the part caudal to the flexure becomes the hindbrain (rhombencephalon).
Human brain — The forebrain separates into two vesicles – an anterior telencephalon and a posterior diencephalon.
Human brain — The telencephalon gives rise to the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and related structures.
Human brain — The hindbrain also splits into two areas – the metencephalon and the myelencephalon.
Human brain — Also during the fifth week, the brain divides into repeating segments called neuromeres.
Human brain — By the gestational age of 24 weeks, the wrinkled morphology showing the fissures that begin to mark out the lobes of the brain is evident.
Human brain — Why the cortex wrinkles and folds is not well-understood, but gyrification has been linked to intelligence and neurological disorders, and a number of gyrification theories have been proposed.
Human brain — These theories include those based on mechanical buckling, axonal tension, and differential tangential expansion.
Human brain — What is clear is that gyrification is not a random process, but rather a complex developmentally predetermined process which generates patterns of folds that are consistent between individuals and most species.
Human brain — The expanding caudal end of the hemisphere has to curve over in a forward direction to fit into the restricted space.
Human brain — This covers the fossa and turns it into a much deeper ridge known as the lateral sulcus and this marks out the temporal lobe.
Human brain — By the sixth month other sulci have formed that demarcate the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes.
Human brain — A gene present in the human genome (ARHGAP11B) may play a major role in gyrification and encephalisation.
Human brain — === Motor control === The frontal lobe is involved in reasoning, motor control, emotion, and language.
Human brain — It contains the motor cortex, which is involved in planning and coordinating movement; the prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for higher-level cognitive functioning; and Broca's area, which is essential for language production.
Human brain — The motor system of the brain is responsible for the generation and control of movement.
Human brain — Generated movements pass from the brain through nerves to motor neurons in the body, which control the action of muscles.
Human brain — The corticospinal tract carries movements from the brain, through the spinal cord, to the torso and limbs.
Human brain — Gross movement – such as locomotion and the movement of arms and legs – is generated in the motor cortex, divided into three parts: the primary motor cortex, found in the precentral gyrus and has sections dedicated to the movement of different body parts.
Human brain — These movements are supported and regulated by two other areas, lying anterior to the primary motor cortex: the premotor area and the supplementary motor area.
Human brain — The hands and mouth have a much larger area dedicated to them than other body parts, allowing finer movement; this has been visualised in a motor homunculus.
Human brain — Impulses generated from the motor cortex travel along the corticospinal tract along the front of the medulla and cross over (decussate) at the medullary pyramids.
Human brain — These then travel down the spinal cord, with most connecting to interneurons, in turn connecting to lower motor neurons within the grey matter that then transmit the impulse to move to muscles themselves.
Human brain — The cerebellum and basal ganglia, play a role in fine, complex and coordinated muscle movements.
Human brain — Connections between the cortex and the basal ganglia control muscle tone, posture and movement initiation, and are referred to as the extrapyramidal system.
Human brain — The sensory nervous system is involved with the reception and processing of sensory information.
Human brain — This information is received through the cranial nerves, through tracts in the spinal cord, and directly at centres of the brain exposed to the blood.
Human brain — The brain also receives and interprets information from the special senses of vision, smell, hearing, and taste.
Human brain — From the skin, the brain receives information about fine touch, pressure, pain, vibration and temperature.
Human brain — The sensory cortex is found just near the motor cortex, and, like the motor cortex, has areas related to sensation from different body parts.
Human brain — Sensation collected by a sensory receptor on the skin is changed to a nerve signal, that is passed up a series of neurons through tracts in the spinal cord.
Human brain — The dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway contains information about fine touch, vibration and position of joints.
Human brain — The pathway fibres travel up the back part of the spinal cord to the back part of the medulla, where they connect with second-order neurons that immediately send fibres across the midline.
Human brain — These fibres then travel upwards into the ventrobasal complex in the thalamus where they connect with third-order neurons which send fibres up to the sensory cortex.
Human brain — The spinothalamic tract carries information about pain, temperature, and gross touch.
Human brain — The pathway fibres travel up the spinal cord and connect with second-order neurons in the reticular formation of the brainstem for pain and temperature, and also terminate at the ventrobasal complex of the thalamus for gross touch.
Human brain — Photoreceptors in the retina transduce the sensory stimulus of light into an electrical nerve signal that is sent to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
Human brain — The arrangements of the eyes' optics cause light from the left visual field to be received by the rightmost portion of each retina, and vice versa.
Human brain — This arrangement ultimately means that a portion of each retina is processed by each hemisphere of the cortex, such that both the right and left visual cortex process information from both eyes.
Human brain — Optic nerve fibres from the retinas' nasal halves cross to the opposite sides joining the fibres from the temporal halves of the opposite retinas, which do not cross, forming the optic tracts.
Human brain — The optic tract fibres reach the brain at the lateral geniculate nucleus, and travel through the optic radiation to reach the visual cortex.
Human brain — Sound results in vibrations of the ossicles which continue finally to the hearing organ, and change in balance results in movement of liquids within the inner ear.
Human brain — From here, it passes through to the cochlear nuclei, the superior olivary nucleus, the medial geniculate nucleus, and finally the auditory radiation to the auditory cortex.
Human brain — The sense of smell is generated by receptor cells in the epithelium of the olfactory mucosa in the nasal cavity.
Human brain — This information passes via the olfactory nerve which goes into the skull through a relatively permeable part.
Human brain — This nerve transmits to the neural circuitry of the olfactory bulb from where information is passed to the olfactory cortex.
Human brain — Taste is generated from receptors on the tongue and passed along the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves into the solitary nucleus in the brainstem.
Human brain — Some taste information is also passed from the pharynx into this area via the vagus nerve.
Human brain — Information is then passed from here through the thalamus into the gustatory cortex.
Human brain — === Regulation === Autonomic functions of the brain include the regulation, or rhythmic control of the heart rate and rate of breathing, and maintaining homeostasis.
Human brain — Blood pressure and heart rate are influenced by the vasomotor centre of the medulla, which causes arteries and veins to be somewhat constricted at rest.
Human brain — It does this by influencing the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems via the vagus nerve.
Human brain — Information about blood pressure is generated by baroreceptors in aortic bodies in the aortic arch, and passed to the brain along the afferent fibres of the vagus nerve.
Human brain — Information about the pressure changes in the carotid sinus comes from carotid bodies located near the carotid artery and this is passed via a nerve joining with the glossopharyngeal nerve.
Human brain — Signals from here influence the vasomotor centre to adjust vein and artery constriction accordingly.
Human brain — The brain controls the rate of breathing, mainly by respiratory centres in the medulla and pons.
Human brain — The respiratory centres control respiration, by generating motor signals that are passed down the spinal cord, along the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm and other muscles of respiration.
Human brain — There are four respiratory centres, three with a more clearly defined function, and an apneustic centre with a less clear function.
Human brain — In the medulla a dorsal respiratory group causes the desire to breathe in and receives sensory information directly from the body.
Human brain — Also in the medulla, the ventral respiratory group influences breathing out during exertion.
Human brain — In the pons the pneumotaxic centre influences the duration of each breath, and the apneustic centre seems to have an influence on inhalation.
Human brain — Information about blood oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH levels are also sensed on the walls of arteries in the peripheral chemoreceptors of the aortic and carotid bodies.
Human brain — This information is passed via the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves to the respiratory centres.
Human brain — High carbon dioxide, an acidic pH, or low oxygen stimulate the respiratory centres.
