k-d tree — In computer science, a k-d tree (short for k-dimensional tree) is a space-partitioning data structure for organizing points in a k-dimensional space.
k-d tree — K-dimensional is that which concerns exactly k orthogonal axes or a space of any number of dimensions. k-d trees are a useful data structure for several applications, such as:
k-d tree — Searches involving a multidimensional search key (e.g. range searches and nearest neighbor searches) & Creating point clouds. k-d trees are a special case of binary space partitioning trees.
k-d tree — == Description == The k-d tree is a binary tree in which every node is a k-dimensional point.
k-d tree — Every non-leaf node can be thought of as implicitly generating a splitting hyperplane that divides the space into two parts, known as half-spaces.
k-d tree — Points to the left of this hyperplane are represented by the left subtree of that node and points to the right of the hyperplane are represented by the right subtree.
k-d tree — The hyperplane direction is chosen in the following way: every node in the tree is associated with one of the k dimensions, with the hyperplane perpendicular to that dimension's axis.
k-d tree — So, for example, if for a particular split the "x" axis is chosen, all points in the subtree with a smaller "x" value than the node will appear in the left subtree and all points with a larger "x" value will be in the right subtree.
k-d tree — In such a case, the hyperplane would be set by the x value of the point, and its normal would be the unit x-axis.
k-d tree — === Construction === Since there are many possible ways to choose axis-aligned splitting planes, there are many different ways to construct k-d trees.
k-d tree — As one moves down the tree, one cycles through the axes used to select the splitting planes. (For example, in a 3-dimensional tree, the root would have an x-aligned plane, the root's children would both have y-aligned planes, the root's grandchildren would all have z-aligned planes, the root's great-grandchildren would all have x-aligned planes, the root's great-great-grandchildren would all have y-aligned planes, and so on.) Points are inserted by selecting the median of the points being put into the subtree, with respect to their coordinates in the axis being used to create the splitting plane. (Note the assumption that we feed the entire set of n points into the algorithm up-front.) This method leads to a balanced k-d tree, in which each leaf node is approximately the same distance from the root.
k-d tree — In the case where median points are not selected, there is no guarantee that the tree will be balanced.
k-d tree — To avoid coding a complex O ( n ) {\displaystyle O(n)} median-finding algorithm or using an O ( n log ⁡ ( n ) ) {\displaystyle O(n\log(n))} sort such as heapsort or mergesort to sort all n points, a popular practice is to sort a fixed number of randomly selected points, and use the median of those points to serve as the splitting plane.
k-d tree — Given a list of n points, the following algorithm uses a median-finding sort to construct a balanced k-d tree containing those points.
k-d tree — function kdtree (list of points pointList, int depth) { // Select axis based on depth so that axis cycles through all valid values var int axis := depth mod k;
k-d tree — // Sort point list and choose median as pivot element select median by axis from pointList;
k-d tree — // Create node and construct subtree node.location := median; node.leftChild := kdtree(points in pointList before median, depth+1); node.rightChild := kdtree(points in pointList after median, depth+1); return node; }
k-d tree — It is common that points "after" the median include only the ones that are strictly greater than the median in the current dimension.
k-d tree — For points that lie on the median in the current dimension, it is possible to define a function that compares them in all dimensions.
k-d tree — In some cases, it is acceptable to let points equal to the median lie on one side of the median, for example, by splitting the points into a "lesser than" subset and a "greater than or equal to" subset.
k-d tree — This algorithm creates the invariant that for any node, all the nodes in the left subtree are on one side of a splitting plane, and all the nodes in the right subtree are on the other side.
k-d tree — The splitting plane of a node goes through the point associated with that node (referred to in the code as node.location).
k-d tree — Alternative algorithms for building a balanced k-d tree presort the data prior to building the tree.
k-d tree — Then, they maintain the order of the presort during tree construction and hence eliminate the costly step of finding the median at each level of subdivision.
k-d tree — Two such algorithms build a balanced k-d tree to sort triangles in order to improve the execution time of ray tracing for three-dimensional computer graphics.
k-d tree — These algorithms presort n triangles prior to building the k-d tree, then build the tree in O ( n log ⁡ n ) {\displaystyle O(n\log n)} time in the best case.
k-d tree — An algorithm that builds a balanced k-d tree to sort points has a worst-case complexity of O ( k n log ⁡ ( n ) ) {\displaystyle O(kn\log(n))} .
k-d tree — This algorithm presorts n points in each of k dimensions using an O ( n log ⁡ ( n ) ) {\displaystyle O(n\log(n))} sort such as Heapsort or Mergesort prior to building the tree.
k-d tree — It then maintains the order of these k presorts during tree construction and thereby avoids finding the median at each level of subdivision.
k-d tree — One adds a new point to a k-d tree in the same way as one adds an element to any other search tree.
k-d tree — First, traverse the tree, starting from the root and moving to either the left or the right child depending on whether the point to be inserted is on the "left" or "right" side of the splitting plane.
k-d tree — Once you get to the node under which the child should be located, add the new point as either the left or right child of the leaf node, again depending on which side of the node's splitting plane contains the new node.
k-d tree — Adding points in this manner can cause the tree to become unbalanced, leading to decreased tree performance.
k-d tree — The rate of tree performance degradation is dependent upon the spatial distribution of tree points being added, and the number of points added in relation to the tree size.
k-d tree — If a tree becomes too unbalanced, it may need to be re-balanced to restore the performance of queries that rely on the tree balancing, such as nearest neighbour searching.
k-d tree — To remove a point from an existing k-d tree without breaking the invariant, the easiest way is to form the set of all nodes and leaves from the children of the target node and recreate that part of the tree.
k-d tree — For the general case, find a replacement point, say p {\displaystyle p} , from the subtree rooted at R {\displaystyle R} .
k-d tree — For finding a replacement point, if R {\displaystyle R} discriminates on x {\displaystyle x} (say) and R {\displaystyle R} has a right child, find the point with the minimum x {\displaystyle x} value from the subtree rooted at the right child.
k-d tree — Otherwise, find the point with the maximum x {\displaystyle x} value from the subtree rooted at the left child.
k-d tree — === Balancing === Balancing a k-d tree requires care because k-d trees are sorted in multiple dimensions, so the tree-rotation technique cannot be used to balance them as this may break the invariant.
k-d tree — They include divided k-d tree, pseudo k-d tree, K-D-B-tree, hB-tree and Bkd-tree.
k-d tree — The nearest neighbour search (NN) algorithm aims to find the point in the tree that is nearest to a given input point.
k-d tree — This search can be done efficiently by using the tree properties to quickly eliminate large portions of the search space.
k-d tree — Starting with the root node, the algorithm moves down the tree recursively, in the same way that it would if the search point were being inserted (i.e. it goes left or right depending on whether the point is lesser than or greater than the current node in the split dimension).
k-d tree — Once the algorithm reaches a leaf node, it checks the node point and if the distance is better than the "current best", that node point is saved as the "current best".
k-d tree — The algorithm unwinds the recursion of the tree, performing the following steps at each node: If the current node is closer than the current best, then it becomes the current best.
k-d tree — The algorithm checks whether there could be any points on the other side of the splitting plane that are closer to the search point than the current best.
k-d tree — In concept, this is done by intersecting the splitting hyperplane with a hypersphere around the search point that has a radius equal to the current nearest distance.
k-d tree — Since the hyperplanes are all axis-aligned this is implemented as a simple comparison to see whether the distance between the splitting coordinate of the search point and current node is less than the distance (overall coordinates) from the search point to the current best.
k-d tree — If the hypersphere crosses the plane, there could be nearer points on the other side of the plane, so the algorithm must move down the other branch of the tree from the current node looking for closer points, following the same recursive process as the entire search.
k-d tree — If the hypersphere doesn't intersect the splitting plane, then the algorithm continues walking up the tree, and the entire branch on the other side of that node is eliminated.
k-d tree — When the algorithm finishes this process for the root node, then the search is complete.
k-d tree — Generally the algorithm uses squared distances for comparison to avoid computing square roots.
k-d tree — Additionally, it can save computation by holding the squared current best distance in a variable for comparison.
k-d tree — It can provide the k nearest neighbours to a point by maintaining k current bests instead of just one.
k-d tree — A branch is only eliminated when k points have been found and the branch cannot have points closer than any of the k current bests.
k-d tree — For example, approximate nearest neighbour searching can be achieved by simply setting an upper bound on the number of points to examine in the tree or by interrupting the search process based upon a real time clock (which may be more appropriate in hardware implementations).
k-d tree — The nearest neighbour for points that are already in the tree can be achieved by not updating the refinement for nodes that give zero distance.
k-d tree — As a result, this has the downside of discarding points that are not unique but are co-located with the original search point.
k-d tree — Approximate nearest neighbour is useful in real-time applications such as robotics due to the significant speed increase gained by not searching for the best point exhaustively.
k-d tree — For example, if a tree is storing values corresponding to income and age, then a range search might be something like looking for all members of the tree which have an age between 20 and 50 years and an income between 50,000 and 80,000.
k-d tree — Since k-d trees divide the range of a domain in half at each level of the tree, they are useful for performing range searches.
k-d tree — Analyses of binary search trees has found that the worst case time for range search in a k-dimensional k-d tree containing n nodes is given by the following equation.
k-d tree — t worst = O ( k ⋅ n 1 − 1 k ) {\displaystyle t_{\text{worst}}=O\left(k\cdot n^{1-{\frac {1}{k}}}\right)}
k-d tree — == Degradation in performance with high-dimensional data == Finding the nearest point is an O ( log ⁡ ( n ) ) {\displaystyle O(\log(n))} operation on average, in the case of randomly distributed points, although analysis in general is tricky.
k-d tree — In high-dimensional spaces, the curse of dimensionality causes the algorithm to need to visit many more branches than in lower-dimensional spaces.
k-d tree — In particular, when the number of points is only slightly higher than the number of dimensions, the algorithm is only slightly better than a linear search of all of the points.
k-d tree — As a general rule, if the dimensionality is k, the number of points in the data, n, should be n ≫ 2 k {\displaystyle n\gg 2^{k}} .
k-d tree — Otherwise, when k-d trees are used with high-dimensional data, most of the points in the tree will be evaluated and the efficiency is no better than exhaustive search, and, if a good-enough fast answer is required, approximate nearest-neighbour methods should be used instead.
k-d tree — == Degradation in performance when the query point is far from points in the k-d tree == Additionally, even in low-dimensional space, if the average pairwise distance between the k nearest neighbors of the query point is significantly less than the average distance between the query point and each of the k nearest neighbors, the performance of nearest neighbor search degrades towards linear, since the distances from the query point to each nearest neighbor are of similar magnitude. (In the worst case, consider a cloud of points distributed on the surface of a sphere centered at the origin.
k-d tree — Every point is equidistant from the origin, so a search for the nearest neighbor from the origin would have to iterate through all points on the surface of the sphere to identify the nearest neighbor – which in this case is not even unique.) To mitigate the potentially significant performance degradation of a k-d tree search in the worst case, a maximum distance parameter can be provided to the tree search algorithm, and the recursive search can be pruned whenever the closest point in a given branch of the tree cannot be closer than this maximum distance.
k-d tree — This may result in a nearest neighbor search failing to return a nearest neighbor, which means no points are within this maximum distance from the query point.
k-d tree — == Complexity == Building a static k-d tree from n points has the following worst-case complexity: O(n log2 n) if an O(n log n) sort such as Heapsort or Mergesort is used to find the median at each level of the nascent tree; O(n log n) if an O(n) median of medians algorithm is used to select the median at each level of the nascent tree; O(kn log n) if n points are presorted in each of k dimensions using an O(n log n) sort such as Heapsort or Mergesort prior to building the k-d tree.
k-d tree — Querying an axis-parallel range in a balanced k-d tree takes O(n1−1/k +m) time, where m is the number of the reported points, and k the dimension of the k-d tree.
k-d tree — Finding 1 nearest neighbour in a balanced k-d tree with randomly distributed points takes O(log n) time on average.
k-d tree — === Volumetric objects === Instead of points, a k-d tree can also contain rectangles or hyperrectangles.
k-d tree — Thus range search becomes the problem of returning all rectangles intersecting the search rectangle.
k-d tree — In an orthogonal range search, the opposite coordinate is used when comparing against the median.
k-d tree — For example, if the current level is split along xhigh, we check the xlow coordinate of the search rectangle.
k-d tree — If the median is less than the xlow coordinate of the search rectangle, then no rectangle in the left branch can ever intersect with the search rectangle and so can be pruned.
k-d tree — === Points only in leaves === It is also possible to define a k-d tree with points stored solely in leaves.
k-d tree — This form of k-d tree allows a variety of split mechanics other than the standard median split.
k-d tree — The midpoint splitting rule selects on the middle of the longest axis of the space being searched, regardless of the distribution of points.
k-d tree — This guarantees that the aspect ratio will be at most 2:1, but the depth is dependent on the distribution of points.
k-d tree — A variation, called sliding-midpoint, only splits on the middle if there are points on both sides of the split.
k-d tree — Maneewongvatana and Mount show that this offers "good enough" performance on common data sets.
k-d tree — Using sliding-midpoint, an approximate nearest neighbour query can be answered in O ( 1 ϵ d log ⁡ n ) {\displaystyle O\left({\tfrac {1}{{\epsilon \ }^{d}}}\log n\right)} .
k-d tree — Approximate range counting can be answered in O ( log ⁡ n + ( 1 ϵ ) d ) {\displaystyle O\left(\log n+{\left({\tfrac {1}{\epsilon \ }}\right)}^{d}\right)} with this method.
k-d tree — implicit k-d tree, a k-d tree defined by an implicit splitting function rather than an explicitly-stored set of splits min/max k-d tree, a k-d tree that associates a minimum and maximum value with each of its nodes Relaxed k-d tree, a k-d tree such that the discriminants in each node are arbitrary Related variations:
k-d tree — Quadtree, a space-partitioning structure that splits in two dimensions simultaneously, so that each node has 4 children Octree, a space-partitioning structure that splits in three dimensions simultaneously, so that each node has 8 children Ball tree, a multi-dimensional space partitioning useful for nearest neighbor search R-tree and bounding interval hierarchy, structure for partitioning objects rather than points, with overlapping regions Vantage-point tree, a variant of a k-d tree that uses hyperspheres instead of hyperplanes to partition the data Problems that can be addressed with k-d trees:
k-d tree — Recursive partitioning, a technique for constructing statistical decision trees that are similar to k-d trees Klee's measure problem, a problem of computing the area of a union of rectangles, solvable using k-d trees Guillotine problem, a problem of finding a k-d tree whose cells are large enough to contain a given set of rectangles
k-d tree — == Open source implementations == ALGLIB has C# and C++ implementations of k-d tree based nearest neighbor and approximate nearest neighbor algorithms CGAL the Computational Algorithms Library, has an implementations of k-d tree based nearest neighbor, approximate nearest neighbor as well as range search algorithms.
k-d tree — SciPy, a Python library for scientific computing, contains implementations of k-d tree based nearest neighbor lookup algorithms. scikit-learn, a Python library for machine learning, contains implementations of k-d trees to back nearest neighbor and radius neighbors searches.
Quadtree — A quadtree is a tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly four children.
Quadtree — Quadtrees are the two-dimensional analog of octrees and are most often used to partition a two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions.
Quadtree — The data associated with a leaf cell varies by application, but the leaf cell represents a "unit of interesting spatial information".
Quadtree — The subdivided regions may be square or rectangular, or may have arbitrary shapes.
Quadtree — A tree-pyramid (T-pyramid) is a "complete" tree; every node of the T-pyramid has four child nodes except leaf nodes; all leaves are on the same level, the level that corresponds to individual pixels in the image.
Quadtree — The data in a tree-pyramid can be stored compactly in an array as an implicit data structure similar to the way a binary heap can store a complete binary tree compactly in an array.
Quadtree — Quadtrees may be classified according to the type of data they represent, including areas, points, lines and curves.
Quadtree — Quadtrees may also be classified by whether the shape of the tree is independent of the order in which data is processed.
Quadtree — === Region quadtree === The region quadtree represents a partition of space in two dimensions by decomposing the region into four equal quadrants, subquadrants, and so on with each leaf node containing data corresponding to a specific subregion.
Quadtree — Each node in the tree either has exactly four children, or has no children (a leaf node).
Quadtree — The height of quadtrees that follow this decomposition strategy (i.e. subdividing subquadrants as long as there is interesting data in the subquadrant for which more refinement is desired) is sensitive to and dependent on the spatial distribution of interesting areas in the space being decomposed.
Quadtree — A region quadtree with a depth of n may be used to represent an image consisting of 2n × 2n pixels, where each pixel value is 0 or 1.
Quadtree — In this application, each leaf node represents a block of pixels that are all 0s or all 1s.
Quadtree — Note the potential savings in terms of space when these trees are used for storing images; images often have many regions of considerable size that have the same colour value throughout.
Quadtree — Rather than store a big 2-D array of every pixel in the image, a quadtree can capture the same information potentially many divisive levels higher than the pixel-resolution sized cells that we would otherwise require.
Quadtree — A region quadtree may also be used as a variable resolution representation of a data field.
Quadtree — For example, the temperatures in an area may be stored as a quadtree, with each leaf node storing the average temperature over the subregion it represents.
Quadtree — === Point quadtree === The point quadtree is an adaptation of a binary tree used to represent two-dimensional point data.
Quadtree — It shares the features of all quadtrees but is a true tree as the center of a subdivision is always on a point.
Quadtree — It is often very efficient in comparing two-dimensional, ordered data points, usually operating in O(log n) time.
Quadtree — Point quadtrees are worth mentioning for completeness, but they have been surpassed by k-d trees as tools for generalized binary search.
Quadtree — Point quadtrees with random insertion have been studied under the name weighted planar stochastic lattices.
Quadtree — Given the next point to insert, we find the cell in which it lies and add it to the tree.
Quadtree — The new point is added such that the cell that contains it is divided into quadrants by the vertical and horizontal lines that run through the point.
Quadtree — Since the division of the plane is decided by the order of point-insertion, the tree's height is sensitive to and dependent on insertion order.
Quadtree — Inserting in a "bad" order can lead to a tree of height linear in the number of input points (at which point it becomes a linked-list).
Quadtree — If the point-set is static, pre-processing can be done to create a tree of balanced height.
Quadtree — ==== Node structure for a point quadtree ==== A node of a point quadtree is similar to a node of a binary tree, with the major difference being that it has four pointers (one for each quadrant) instead of two ("left" and "right") as in an ordinary binary tree.
Quadtree — Also a key is usually decomposed into two parts, referring to x and y coordinates.
Quadtree — four pointers: quad[‘NW’], quad[‘NE’], quad[‘SW’], and quad[‘SE’] point; which in turn contains: key; usually expressed as x, y coordinates value; for example a name
Quadtree — === Point-region (PR) quadtree === Point-region (PR) quadtrees are very similar to region quadtrees.
Quadtree — In a region quadtree, a uniform value is stored that applies to the entire area of the cell of a leaf.
Quadtree — The cells of a PR quadtree, however, store a list of points that exist within the cell of a leaf.
Quadtree — As mentioned previously, for trees following this decomposition strategy the height depends on the spatial distribution of the points.
Quadtree — Like the point quadtree, the PR quadtree may also have a linear height when given a "bad" set.
Quadtree — === Edge quadtree === Edge quadtrees (much like PM quadtrees) are used to store lines rather than points.
Quadtree — Curves are approximated by subdividing cells to a very fine resolution, specifically until there is a single line segment per cell.
Quadtree — Near corners/vertices, edge quadtrees will continue dividing until they reach their maximum level of decomposition.
Quadtree — This can result in extremely unbalanced trees which may defeat the purpose of indexing.
Quadtree — === Polygonal map (PM) quadtree === The polygonal map quadtree (or PM Quadtree) is a variation of quadtree which is used to store collections of polygons that may be degenerate (meaning that they have isolated vertices or edges).
Quadtree — A big difference between PM quadtrees and edge quadtrees is that the cell under consideration is not subdivided if the segments meet at a vertex in the cell.
Quadtree — There are three main classes of PM Quadtrees, which vary depending on what information they store within each black node.
Quadtree — PM3 quadtrees can store any amount of non-intersecting edges and at most one point.
Quadtree — PM2 quadtrees are the same as PM3 quadtrees except that all edges must share the same end point.
Quadtree — Finally PM1 quadtrees are similar to PM2, but black nodes can contain a point and its edges or just a set of edges that share a point, but you cannot have a point and a set of edges that do not contain the point.
Quadtree — === Compressed quadtrees === This section summarizes a subsection from a book by Sariel Har-Peled.
Quadtree — If we were to store every node corresponding to a subdivided cell, we may end up storing a lot of empty nodes.
Quadtree — We can cut down on the size of such sparse trees by only storing subtrees whose leaves have interesting data (i.e. "important subtrees").
Quadtree — When we only keep important subtrees, the pruning process may leave long paths in the tree where the intermediate nodes have degree two (a link to one parent and one child).
Quadtree — It turns out that we only need to store the node u {\displaystyle u} at the beginning of this path (and associate some meta-data with it to represent the removed nodes) and attach the subtree rooted at its end to u {\displaystyle u} .
Quadtree — It is still possible for these compressed trees to have a linear height when given "bad" input points.
Quadtree — Although we trim a lot of the tree when we perform this compression, it is still possible to achieve logarithmic-time search, insertion, and deletion by taking advantage of Z-order curves.
Quadtree — The Z-order curve maps each cell of the full quadtree (and hence even the compressed quadtree) in O ( 1 ) {\displaystyle O(1)} time to a one-dimensional line (and maps it back in O ( 1 ) {\displaystyle O(1)} time too), creating a total order on the elements.
Quadtree — Therefore, we can store the quadtree in a data structure for ordered sets (in which we store the nodes of the tree).
Quadtree — We must state a reasonable assumption before we continue: we assume that given two real numbers α , β ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) {\displaystyle \alpha ,\beta \in [0,1)} expressed as binary, we can compute in O ( 1 ) {\displaystyle O(1)} time the index of the first bit in which they differ.
Quadtree — We also assume that we can compute in O ( 1 ) {\displaystyle O(1)} time the lowest common ancestor of two points/cells in the quadtree and establish their relative Z-ordering, and we can compute the floor function in O ( 1 ) {\displaystyle O(1)} time.
Quadtree — With these assumptions, point location of a given point q {\displaystyle q} (i.e. determining the cell that would contain q {\displaystyle q} ), insertion, and deletion operations can all be performed in O ( log ⁡ n ) {\displaystyle O(\log {n})} time (i.e. the time it takes to do a search in the underlying ordered set data structure).
Quadtree — To perform a point location for q {\displaystyle q} (i.e. find its cell in the compressed tree):
Quadtree — Find the existing cell in the compressed tree that comes before q {\displaystyle q} in the Z-order.
Quadtree — Else, find what would have been the lowest common ancestor of the point q {\displaystyle q} and the cell v {\displaystyle v} in an uncompressed quadtree.
Quadtree — Find the existing cell in the compressed tree that comes before u {\displaystyle u} in the Z-order and return it.
Quadtree — Without going into specific details, to perform insertions and deletions we first do a point location for the thing we want to insert/delete, and then insert/delete it.
Quadtree — Care must be taken to reshape the tree as appropriate, creating and removing nodes as needed.

Quadtree — == Image processing using quadtrees == Quadtrees, particularly the region quadtree, have lent themselves well to image processing applications.
Quadtree — We will limit our discussion to binary image data, though region quadtrees and the image processing operations performed on them are just as suitable for colour images.
Quadtree — === Image union / intersection === One of the advantages of using quadtrees for image manipulation is that the set operations of union and intersection can be done simply and quickly.
Quadtree — Given two binary images, the image union (also called overlay) produces an image wherein a pixel is black if either of the input images has a black pixel in the same location.
Quadtree — That is, a pixel in the output image is white only when the corresponding pixel in both input images is white, otherwise the output pixel is black.
Quadtree — Rather than do the operation pixel by pixel, we can compute the union more efficiently by leveraging the quadtree's ability to represent multiple pixels with a single node.
Quadtree — For the purposes of discussion below, if a subtree contains both black and white pixels we will say that the root of that subtree is coloured grey.
Quadtree — The algorithm works by traversing the two input quadtrees ( T 1 {\displaystyle T_{1}} and T 2 {\displaystyle T_{2}} ) while building the output quadtree T {\displaystyle T} .
Quadtree — Consider the nodes v 1 ∈ T 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}\in T_{1}} and v 2 ∈ T 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}\in T_{2}} corresponding to the same region in the images.
Quadtree — If v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} or v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} is black, the corresponding node is created in T {\displaystyle T} and is colored black.
Quadtree — If only one of them is black and the other is gray, the gray node will contain a subtree underneath.
Quadtree — If v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} (respectively, v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} ) is white, v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} (respectively, v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} ) and the subtree underneath it (if any) is copied to T {\displaystyle T} .
Quadtree — If both v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} and v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} are gray, then the corresponding children of v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} and v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} are considered.
Quadtree — While this algorithm works, it does not by itself guarantee a minimally sized quadtree.
Quadtree — For example, consider the result if we were to union a checkerboard (where every tile is a pixel) of size 2 k × 2 k {\displaystyle 2^{k}\times 2^{k}} with its complement.
Quadtree — The result is a giant black square which should be represented by a quadtree with just the root node (coloured black), but instead the algorithm produces a full 4-ary tree of depth k {\displaystyle k} .
Quadtree — To fix this, we perform a bottom-up traversal of the resulting quadtree where we check if the four children nodes have the same colour, in which case we replace their parent with a leaf of the same colour.
Quadtree — One way to think about the intersection of the two images is that we are doing a union with respect to the white pixels.
Quadtree — As such, to perform the intersection we swap the mentions of black and white in the union algorithm.
Quadtree — === Connected component labelling === Consider two neighbouring black pixels in a binary image.
Quadtree — In general, two black pixels are connected if one can be reached from the other by moving only to adjacent pixels (i.e. there is a path of black pixels between them where each consecutive pair is adjacent).
Quadtree — Using the quadtree representation of images, Samet showed how we can find and label these connected components in time proportional to the size of the quadtree.
Quadtree — establish the adjacency relationships between black pixels process the equivalence relations from the first step to obtain one unique label for each connected component label the black pixels with the label associated with their connected component To simplify the discussion, let us assume the children of a node in the quadtree follow the Z-order (SW, NW, SE, NE).
Quadtree — Since we can count on this structure, for any cell we know how to navigate the quadtree to find the adjacent cells in the different levels of the hierarchy.
Quadtree — For each black leaf v {\displaystyle v} we look at the node or nodes representing cells that are Northern neighbours and Eastern neighbours (i.e. the Northern and Eastern cells that share edges with the cell of v {\displaystyle v} ).
Quadtree — Since the tree is organized in Z-order, we have the invariant that the Southern and Western neighbours have already been taken care of and accounted for.
Quadtree — Let the Northern or Eastern neighbour currently under consideration be u {\displaystyle u} .
Quadtree — If only one of u {\displaystyle u} or v {\displaystyle v} has a label, assign that label to the other cell If neither of them have labels, create one and assign it to both of them If u {\displaystyle u} and v {\displaystyle v} have different labels, record this label equivalence and move on Step two can be accomplished using the union-find data structure.
Quadtree — For every equivalence relation noted in the first step, we union the corresponding sets.
Quadtree — Afterwards, each distinct remaining set will be associated with a distinct connected component in the image.
Quadtree — This time, for each black node v {\displaystyle v} we use the union-find's find operation (with the old label of v {\displaystyle v} ) to find and assign v {\displaystyle v} its new label (associated with the connected component of which v {\displaystyle v} is part).
Quadtree — == Mesh generation using quadtrees == This section summarizes a chapter from a book by Har-Peled and de Berg et al.
Quadtree — Mesh generation is essentially the triangulation of a point set for which further processing may be performed.
Quadtree — As such, it is desirable for the resulting triangulation to have certain properties (like non-uniformity, triangles that are not "too skinny", large triangles in sparse areas and small triangles in dense ones, etc.) to make further processing quicker and less error-prone.
Quadtree — Quadtrees built on the point set can be used to create meshes with these desired properties.
Quadtree — Consider a leaf of the quadtree and its corresponding cell v {\displaystyle v} .
Quadtree — We say v {\displaystyle v} is balanced (for mesh generation) if the cell's sides are intersected by the corner points of neighbouring cells at most once on each side.
Quadtree — This means that the quadtree levels of leaves adjacent to v {\displaystyle v} differ by at most one from the level of v {\displaystyle v} .
Quadtree — When this is true for all leaves, we say the whole quadtree is balanced (for mesh generation).
Quadtree — Consider the cell v {\displaystyle v} and the 5 × 5 {\displaystyle 5\times 5} neighbourhood of same-sized cells centred at v {\displaystyle v} .
Quadtree — We say the quadtree is well-balanced if it is balanced, and for every leaf u {\displaystyle u} that contains a point of the point set, its extended cluster is also in the quadtree and the extended cluster contains no other point of the point set.
Quadtree — For every leaf, if there is a neighbour that is too large, subdivide the neighbour.
Quadtree — We also make sure that for a leaf with a point in it, the nodes for each leaf's extended cluster are in the tree.
Quadtree — For every leaf node v {\displaystyle v} that contains a point, if the extended cluster contains another point, we further subdivide the tree and rebalance as necessary.
Quadtree — If we needed to subdivide, for each child u {\displaystyle u} of v {\displaystyle v} we ensure the nodes of u {\displaystyle u} 's extended cluster are in the tree (and re-balance as required).
Quadtree — We consider the corner points of the tree cells as vertices in our triangulation.
Quadtree — Before the transformation step we have a bunch of boxes with points in some of them.
Quadtree — The transformation step is done in the following manner: for each point, warp the closest corner of its cell to meet it and triangulate the resulting four quadrangles to make "nice" triangles (the interested reader is referred to chapter 12 of Har-Peled for more details on what makes "nice" triangles).
Quadtree — For each regular square (no points within and no corner points in its sides), introduce the diagonal.
Quadtree — Due to the way in which we separated points with the well-balancing property, no square with a corner intersecting a side is one that was warped.
Quadtree — If there is one intersected side, the square becomes three triangles by adding the long diagonals connecting the intersection with opposite corners.
Quadtree — If there are four intersected sides, we split the square in half by adding an edge between two of the four intersections, and then connect these two endpoints to the remaining two intersection points.
Quadtree — For the other squares, we introduce a point in the middle and connect it to all four corners of the square as well as each intersection point.
Quadtree — At the end of it all, we have a nice triangulated mesh of our point set built from a quadtree.

R-tree — R-trees are tree data structures used for spatial access methods, i.e., for indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons.
R-tree — The R-tree was proposed by Antonin Guttman in 1984 and has found significant use in both theoretical and applied contexts.
R-tree — A common real-world usage for an R-tree might be to store spatial objects such as restaurant locations or the polygons that typical maps are made of: streets, buildings, outlines of lakes, coastlines, etc. and then find answers quickly to queries such as "Find all museums within 2 km of my current location", "retrieve all road segments within 2 km of my location" (to display them in a navigation system) or "find the nearest gas station" (although not taking roads into account).
R-tree — The R-tree can also accelerate nearest neighbor search for various distance metrics, including great-circle distance.
R-tree — == R-tree idea == The key idea of the data structure is to group nearby objects and represent them with their minimum bounding rectangle in the next higher level of the tree; the "R" in R-tree is for rectangle.
R-tree — Since all objects lie within this bounding rectangle, a query that does not intersect the bounding rectangle also cannot intersect any of the contained objects.
R-tree — At the leaf level, each rectangle describes a single object; at higher levels the aggregation includes an increasing number of objects.
R-tree — Similar to the B-tree, the R-tree is also a balanced search tree (so all leaf nodes are at the same depth), organizes the data in pages, and is designed for storage on disk (as used in databases).
R-tree — Each page can contain a maximum number of entries, often denoted as M {\displaystyle M} .
R-tree — It also guarantees a minimum fill (except for the root node), however best performance has been experienced with a minimum fill of 30%–40% of the maximum number of entries (B-trees guarantee 50% page fill, and B*-trees even 66%).
R-tree — The reason for this is the more complex balancing required for spatial data as opposed to linear data stored in B-trees.
R-tree — As with most trees, the searching algorithms (e.g., intersection, containment, nearest neighbor search) are rather simple.
R-tree — The key idea is to use the bounding boxes to decide whether or not to search inside a subtree.
R-tree — Like B-trees, R-trees are suitable for large data sets and databases, where nodes can be paged to memory when needed, and the whole tree cannot be kept in main memory.
R-tree — Even if data can be fit in memory (or cached), the R-trees in most practical applications will usually provide performance advantages over naive check of all objects when the number of objects is more than few hundred or so.
R-tree — However, for in-memory applications, there are similar alternatives that can provide slightly better performance or be simpler to implement in practice.
R-tree — To maintain in-memory computing for R-tree in a computer cluster where computing nodes are connected by a network, researchers have used RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) to implement data-intensive applications under R-tree in a distributed environment.
R-tree — This approach is scalable for increasingly large applications and achieves high throughput and low latency performance for R-tree.
R-tree — The key difficulty of R-tree is to build an efficient tree that on one hand is balanced (so the leaf nodes are at the same height) on the other hand the rectangles do not cover too much empty space and do not overlap too much (so that during search, fewer subtrees need to be processed).
R-tree — For example, the original idea for inserting elements to obtain an efficient tree is to always insert into the subtree that requires least enlargement of its bounding box.
R-tree — Once that page is full, the data is split into two sets that should cover the minimal area each.
R-tree — Most of the research and improvements for R-trees aims at improving the way the tree is built and can be grouped into two objectives: building an efficient tree from scratch (known as bulk-loading) and performing changes on an existing tree (insertion and deletion).
R-tree — R-trees do not guarantee good worst-case performance, but generally perform well with real-world data.
R-tree — The (bulk-loaded) Priority R-tree variant of the R-tree is worst-case optimal, but due to its increased complexity it has remained confined to theoretical study and has not received much attention in practical applications.
R-tree — When data is organized in an R-tree, the neighbors within a given distance r and the k nearest neighbors (for any Lp-Norm) of all points can efficiently be computed using a spatial join.
R-tree — This is beneficial for many algorithms based on such queries, for example the Local Outlier Factor.
R-tree — DeLi-Clu, Density-Link-Clustering is a cluster analysis algorithm that uses the R-tree structure for a similar kind of spatial join to efficiently compute an OPTICS clustering.
R-tree — === Data layout === Data in R-trees is organized in pages that can have a variable number of entries (up to some pre-defined maximum, and usually above a minimum fill).
R-tree — Each entry within a non-leaf node stores two pieces of data: a way of identifying a child node, and the bounding box of all entries within this child node.
R-tree — Leaf nodes store the data required for each child, often a point or bounding box representing the child and an external identifier for the child.
R-tree — For polygon data (that often requires the storage of large polygons) the common setup is to store only the MBR (minimum bounding rectangle) of the polygon along with a unique identifier in the tree.
R-tree — === Search === The search process in an R-tree embodies a two-phase approach that aligns with the Filter and Refine Principle (FRP).
R-tree — In this structure, the internal nodes serve as an initial filter by quickly excluding regions of space that do not intersect the query, while the leaf nodes provide a refined, precise evaluation by storing the actual spatial objects.
R-tree — Every internal node contains a set of rectangles and pointers to the corresponding child node and every leaf node contains the rectangles of spatial objects (the pointer to some spatial object can be there).
R-tree — For every rectangle in a node, it has to be decided if it overlaps the search rectangle or not.
R-tree — Searching is done like this in a recursive manner until all overlapping nodes have been traversed.
R-tree — When a leaf node is reached, the contained bounding boxes (rectangles) are tested against the search rectangle and their objects (if there are any) are put into the result set if they lie within the search rectangle.
R-tree — For priority search such as nearest neighbor search, the query consists of a point or rectangle.
R-tree — Until the queue is empty or the desired number of results have been returned the search continues by processing the nearest entry in the queue.
R-tree — This approach can be used with various distance metrics, including great-circle distance for geographic data.
R-tree — === Insertion === To insert an object, the tree is traversed recursively from the root node.
R-tree — At each step, all rectangles in the current directory node are examined, and a candidate is chosen using a heuristic such as choosing the rectangle which requires least enlargement.
R-tree — Again, since an exhaustive search is too expensive, a heuristic is employed to split the node into two.
R-tree — Adding the newly created node to the previous level, this level can again overflow, and these overflows can propagate up to the root node; when this node also overflows, a new root node is created and the tree has increased in height.
R-tree — ==== Choosing the insertion subtree ==== The algorithm needs to decide in which subtree to insert.
R-tree — When a data object is fully contained in a single rectangle, the choice is clear.
R-tree — When there are multiple options or rectangles in need of enlargement, the choice can have a significant impact on the performance of the tree.
R-tree — What happens next is it tries to minimize the overlap (in case of ties, prefer least enlargement and then least area); at the higher levels, it behaves similar to the R-tree, but on ties again preferring the subtree with smaller area.
R-tree — The decreased overlap of rectangles in the R*-tree is one of the key benefits over the traditional R-tree.
R-tree — ==== Splitting an overflowing node ==== Since redistributing all objects of a node into two nodes has an exponential number of options, a heuristic needs to be employed to find the best split.
R-tree — In the classic R-tree, Guttman proposed two such heuristics, called QuadraticSplit and LinearSplit.
R-tree — In quadratic split, the algorithm searches for the pair of rectangles that is the worst combination to have in the same node, and puts them as initial objects into the two new groups.
R-tree — It then searches for the entry which has the strongest preference for one of the groups (in terms of area increase) and assigns the object to this group until all objects are assigned (satisfying the minimum fill).
R-tree — There are other splitting strategies such as Greene's Split, the R*-tree splitting heuristic (which again tries to minimize overlap, but also prefers quadratic pages) or the linear split algorithm proposed by Ang and Tan (which however can produce very irregular rectangles, which are less performant for many real world range and window queries).
R-tree — In addition to having a more advanced splitting heuristic, the R*-tree also tries to avoid splitting a node by reinserting some of the node members, which is similar to the way a B-tree balances overflowing nodes.
R-tree — Finally, the X-tree can be seen as a R*-tree variant that can also decide to not split a node, but construct a so-called super-node containing all the extra entries, when it doesn't find a good split (in particular for high-dimensional data).
R-tree — === Deletion === Deleting an entry from a page may require updating the bounding rectangles of parent pages.
R-tree — Instead, the page will be dissolved and all its children (which may be subtrees, not only leaf objects) will be reinserted.
R-tree — If during this process the root node has a single element, the tree height can decrease.
R-tree — === Bulk-loading === Nearest-X: Objects are sorted by their first coordinate ("X") and then split into pages of the desired size.
R-tree — Packed Hilbert R-tree: variation of Nearest-X, but sorting using the Hilbert value of the center of a rectangle instead of using the X coordinate.
R-tree — Sort-Tile-Recursive (STR): Another variation of Nearest-X, that estimates the total number of leaves required as l = ⌈ number of objects / capacity ⌉ {\displaystyle l=\lceil {\text{number of objects}}/{\text{capacity}}\rceil } , the required split factor in each dimension to achieve this as s = ⌈ l 1 / d ⌉ {\displaystyle s=\lceil l^{1/d}\rceil } , then repeatedly splits each dimensions successively into s {\displaystyle s} equal sized partitions using 1-dimensional sorting.
R-tree — The resulting pages, if they occupy more than one page, are again bulk-loaded using the same algorithm.
R-tree — For point data, the leaf nodes will not overlap, and "tile" the data space into approximately equal sized pages.
R-tree — Overlap Minimizing Top-down (OMT): Improvement over STR using a top-down approach which minimizes overlaps between slices and improves query performance.
R-tree — == See also == Segment tree Interval tree – A degenerate R-tree for one dimension (usually time).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In discrete mathematics, particularly in graph theory, a graph is a structure consisting of a set of objects where some pairs of the objects are in some sense "related".
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The objects are represented by abstractions called vertices (also called nodes or points) and each of the related pairs of vertices is called an edge (also called link or line).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Typically, a graph is depicted in diagrammatic form as a set of dots or circles for the vertices, joined by lines or curves for the edges.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — For example, if the vertices represent people at a party, and there is an edge between two people if they shake hands, then this graph is undirected because any person A can shake hands with a person B only if B also shakes hands with A.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In contrast, if an edge from a person A to a person B means that A owes money to B, then this graph is directed, because owing money is not necessarily reciprocated.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Sylvester in 1878 due to a direct relation between mathematics and chemical structure (what he called a chemico-graphical image).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The following are some of the more basic ways of defining graphs and related mathematical structures.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A graph (sometimes called an undirected graph to distinguish it from a directed graph, or a simple graph to distinguish it from a multigraph) is a pair G = (V, E), where V is a set whose elements are called vertices (singular: vertex), and E is a set of unordered pairs { v 1 , v 2 } {\displaystyle \{v_{1},v_{2}\}} of vertices, whose elements are called edges (sometimes links or lines).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A vertex may belong to no edge, in which case it is not joined to any other vertex and is called isolated.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — When an edge { u , v } {\displaystyle \{u,v\}} exists, the vertices u and v are called adjacent.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A multigraph is a generalization that allows multiple edges to have the same pair of endpoints.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Sometimes, graphs are allowed to contain loops, which are edges that join a vertex to itself.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — To allow loops, the pairs of vertices in E must be allowed to have the same node twice.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Such generalized graphs are called graphs with loops or simply graphs when it is clear from the context that loops are allowed.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Generally, the vertex set V is taken to be finite (which implies that the edge set E is also finite).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Sometimes infinite graphs are considered, but they are usually viewed as a special kind of binary relation, because most results on finite graphs either do not extend to the infinite case or need a rather different proof.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — An empty graph is a graph that has an empty set of vertices (and thus an empty set of edges).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — However, in some contexts, such as for expressing the computational complexity of algorithms, the term size is used for the quantity |V| + |E| (otherwise, a non-empty graph could have size 0).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The degree or valency of a vertex is the number of edges that are incident to it; for graphs with loops, a loop is counted twice.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In a graph of order n, the maximum degree of each vertex is n − 1 (or n + 1 if loops are allowed, because a loop contributes 2 to the degree), and the maximum number of edges is n(n − 1)/2 (or n(n + 1)/2 if loops are allowed).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The edges of a graph define a symmetric relation on the vertices, called the adjacency relation.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A graph is fully determined by its adjacency matrix A, which is an n × n square matrix, with Aij specifying the number of connections from vertex i to vertex j.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — For a simple graph, Aij is either 0, indicating disconnection, or 1, indicating connection; moreover Aii = 0 because an edge in a simple graph cannot start and end at the same vertex.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Graphs with self-loops will be characterized by some or all Aii being equal to a positive integer, and multigraphs (with multiple edges between vertices) will be characterized by some or all Aij being equal to a positive integer.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In one restricted but very common sense of the term, a directed graph is a pair G = (V, E) comprising:
Graph (discrete mathematics) — V, a set of vertices (also called nodes or points); E, a set of edges (also called directed edges, directed links, directed lines, arrows, or arcs), which are ordered pairs of distinct vertices: E ⊆ { ( x , y ) ∣ ( x , y ) ∈ V 2 and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle E\subseteq \{(x,y)\mid (x,y)\in V^{2}\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\}} .
Graph (discrete mathematics) — To avoid ambiguity, this type of object may be called precisely a directed simple graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In the edge (x, y) directed from x to y, the vertices x and y are called the endpoints of the edge, x the tail of the edge and y the head of the edge.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Multiple edges, not allowed under the definition above, are two or more edges with both the same tail and the same head.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In one more general sense of the term allowing multiple edges, a directed graph is sometimes defined to be an ordered triple G = (V, E, ϕ) comprising:
Graph (discrete mathematics) — V, a set of vertices (also called nodes or points); E, a set of edges (also called directed edges, directed links, directed lines, arrows or arcs); ϕ, an incidence function mapping every edge to an ordered pair of vertices (that is, an edge is associated with two distinct vertices): ϕ : E → { ( x , y ) ∣ ( x , y ) ∈ V 2 and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle \phi :E\to \{(x,y)\mid (x,y)\in V^{2}\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\}} .
Graph (discrete mathematics) — To avoid ambiguity, this type of object may be called precisely a directed multigraph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Directed graphs as defined in the two definitions above cannot have loops, because a loop joining a vertex x {\displaystyle x} to itself is the edge (for a directed simple graph) or is incident on (for a directed multigraph) ( x , x ) {\displaystyle (x,x)} which is not in { ( x , y ) ∣ ( x , y ) ∈ V 2 and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle \{(x,y)\mid (x,y)\in V^{2}\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\}} .
Graph (discrete mathematics) — For directed simple graphs, the definition of E {\displaystyle E} should be modified to E ⊆ V 2 {\displaystyle E\subseteq V^{2}} .
Graph (discrete mathematics) — For directed multigraphs, the definition of ϕ {\displaystyle \phi } should be modified to ϕ : E → V 2 {\displaystyle \phi :E\to V^{2}} .
Graph (discrete mathematics) — To avoid ambiguity, these types of objects may be called precisely a directed simple graph permitting loops and a directed multigraph permitting loops (or a quiver) respectively.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The edges of a directed simple graph permitting loops G is a homogeneous relation ~ on the vertices of G that is called the adjacency relation of G.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Specifically, for each edge (x, y), its endpoints x and y are said to be adjacent to one another, which is denoted x ~ y.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A mixed graph is a graph in which some edges may be directed and some may be undirected.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — It is an ordered triple G = (V, E, A) for a mixed simple graph and G = (V, E, A, ϕE, ϕA) for a mixed multigraph with V, E (the undirected edges), A (the directed edges), ϕE and ϕA defined as above.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A weighted graph or a network is a graph in which a number (the weight) is assigned to each edge.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Such weights might represent for example costs, lengths or capacities, depending on the problem at hand.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Such graphs arise in many contexts, for example in shortest path problems such as the traveling salesman problem.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — === Oriented graph === One definition of an oriented graph is that it is a directed graph in which at most one of (x, y) and (y, x) may be edges of the graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — That is, it is a directed graph that can be formed as an orientation of an undirected (simple) graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Some authors use "oriented graph" to mean any orientation of a given undirected graph or multigraph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A regular graph is a graph in which each vertex has the same number of neighbours, i.e., every vertex has the same degree.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A regular graph with vertices of degree k is called a k‑regular graph or regular graph of degree k.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A complete graph is a graph in which each pair of vertices is joined by an edge.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — === Finite graph === A finite graph is a graph in which the vertex set and the edge set are finite sets.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Most commonly in graph theory it is implied that the graphs discussed are finite.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In an undirected graph, an unordered pair of vertices {x, y} is called connected if a path leads from x to y.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A connected graph is an undirected graph in which every unordered pair of vertices in the graph is connected.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In a directed graph, an ordered pair of vertices (x, y) is called strongly connected if a directed path leads from x to y.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Otherwise, the ordered pair is called weakly connected if an undirected path leads from x to y after replacing all of its directed edges with undirected edges.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A strongly connected graph is a directed graph in which every ordered pair of vertices in the graph is strongly connected.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Otherwise, it is called a weakly connected graph if every ordered pair of vertices in the graph is weakly connected.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A k-vertex-connected graph or k-edge-connected graph is a graph in which no set of k − 1 vertices (respectively, edges) exists that, when removed, disconnects the graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A bipartite graph is a simple graph in which the vertex set can be partitioned into two sets, W and X, so that no two vertices in W share a common edge and no two vertices in X share a common edge.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In a complete bipartite graph, the vertex set is the union of two disjoint sets, W and X, so that every vertex in W is adjacent to every vertex in X but there are no edges within W or X.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A path graph or linear graph of order n ≥ 2 is a graph in which the vertices can be listed in an order v1, v2, …, vn such that the edges are the {vi, vi+1} where i = 1, 2, …, n − 1.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Path graphs can be characterized as connected graphs in which the degree of all but two vertices is 2 and the degree of the two remaining vertices is 1.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — If a path graph occurs as a subgraph of another graph, it is a path in that graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A planar graph is a graph whose vertices and edges can be drawn in a plane such that no two of the edges intersect.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A cycle graph or circular graph of order n ≥ 3 is a graph in which the vertices can be listed in an order v1, v2, …, vn such that the edges are the {vi, vi+1} where i = 1, 2, …, n − 1, plus the edge {vn, v1}.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Cycle graphs can be characterized as connected graphs in which the degree of all vertices is 2.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — If a cycle graph occurs as a subgraph of another graph, it is a cycle or circuit in that graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A tree is an undirected graph in which any two vertices are connected by exactly one path, or equivalently a connected acyclic undirected graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A forest is an undirected graph in which any two vertices are connected by at most one path, or equivalently an acyclic undirected graph, or equivalently a disjoint union of trees.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A polytree (or directed tree or oriented tree or singly connected network) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose underlying undirected graph is a tree.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A polyforest (or directed forest or oriented forest) is a directed acyclic graph whose underlying undirected graph is a forest.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Petersen graph and its generalizations; perfect graphs; cographs; chordal graphs; other graphs with large automorphism groups: vertex-transitive, arc-transitive, and distance-transitive graphs; strongly regular graphs and their generalizations distance-regular graphs.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Two vertices of a directed graph are called consecutive if the head of the first one is the tail of the second one.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Similarly, two vertices are called adjacent if they share a common edge (consecutive if the first one is the tail and the second one is the head of an edge), in which case the common edge is said to join the two vertices.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The graph with no vertices and no edges is sometimes called the null graph or empty graph, but the terminology is not consistent and not all mathematicians allow this object.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Normally, the vertices of a graph, by their nature as elements of a set, are distinguishable.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — However, for many questions it is better to treat vertices as indistinguishable. (Of course, the vertices may be still distinguishable by the properties of the graph itself, e.g., by the numbers of incident edges.) The same remarks apply to edges, so graphs with labeled edges are called edge-labeled.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Graphs with labels attached to edges or vertices are more generally designated as labeled.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Consequently, graphs in which vertices are indistinguishable and edges are indistinguishable are called unlabeled. (In the literature, the term labeled may apply to other kinds of labeling, besides that which serves only to distinguish different vertices or edges.) The category of directed multigraphs permitting loops is the comma category Set ↓ D where D: Set → Set is the functor taking a set s to s × s.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — The diagram is a schematic representation of the graph with vertices V = { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 } {\displaystyle V=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}} and edges E = { { 1 , 2 } , { 1 , 5 } , { 2 , 3 } , { 2 , 5 } , { 3 , 4 } , { 4 , 5 } , { 4 , 6 } } . {\displaystyle E=\{\{1,2\},\{1,5\},\{2,3\},\{2,5\},\{3,4\},\{4,5\},\{4,6\}\}.}
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In computer science, directed graphs are used to represent knowledge (e.g., conceptual graph), finite-state machines, and many other discrete structures.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — An element x of X is a direct predecessor of an element y of X if and only if xRy.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — A directed graph can model information networks such as Twitter, with one user following another.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — Particularly regular examples of directed graphs are given by the Cayley graphs of finitely-generated groups, as well as Schreier coset graphs In category theory, every small category has an underlying directed multigraph whose vertices are the objects of the category, and whose edges are the arrows of the category.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In the language of category theory, one says that there is a forgetful functor from the category of small categories to the category of quivers.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — There are several operations that produce new graphs from initial ones, which might be classified into the following categories:
Graph (discrete mathematics) — unary operations, which create a new graph from an initial one, such as: edge contraction, line graph, dual graph, complement graph, graph rewriting; binary operations, which create a new graph from two initial ones, such as: disjoint union of graphs, cartesian product of graphs, tensor product of graphs, strong product of graphs, lexicographic product of graphs, series–parallel graphs.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — == Generalizations == In a hypergraph, an edge can join any positive number of vertices.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — An undirected graph can be seen as a simplicial complex consisting of 1-simplices (the edges) and 0-simplices (the vertices).
Graph (discrete mathematics) — As such, complexes are generalizations of graphs since they allow for higher-dimensional simplices.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — But in that case, there is no limitation on the number of edges: it can be any cardinal number, see continuous graph.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In computational biology, power graph analysis introduces power graphs as an alternative representation of undirected graphs.
Graph (discrete mathematics) — In geographic information systems, geometric networks are closely modeled after graphs, and borrow many concepts from graph theory to perform spatial analysis on road networks or utility grids.

Graph theory — In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.
Graph theory — A graph in this context is made up of vertices (also called nodes or points) which are connected by edges (also called arcs, links or lines).
Graph theory — A distinction is made between undirected graphs, where edges link two vertices symmetrically, and directed graphs, where edges link two vertices asymmetrically.
Graph theory — The following are some of the more basic ways of defining graphs and related mathematical structures.
Graph theory — In one restricted but very common sense of the term, a graph is an ordered pair G = ( V , E ) {\displaystyle G=(V,E)} comprising:
Graph theory — E ⊆ { { x , y } ∣ x , y ∈ V and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle E\subseteq \{\{x,y\}\mid x,y\in V\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\}} , a set of edges (also called links or lines), which are unordered pairs of vertices (that is, an edge is associated with two distinct vertices).
Graph theory — To avoid ambiguity, this type of object may be called an undirected simple graph.
Graph theory — In the edge { x , y } {\displaystyle \{x,y\}} , the vertices x {\displaystyle x} and y {\displaystyle y} are called the endpoints of the edge.
Graph theory — The edge is said to join x {\displaystyle x} and y {\displaystyle y} and to be incident on x {\displaystyle x} and on y {\displaystyle y} .
Graph theory — Under this definition, multiple edges, in which two or more edges connect the same vertices, are not allowed.
Graph theory — In one more general sense of the term allowing multiple edges, a graph is an ordered triple G = ( V , E , ϕ ) {\displaystyle G=(V,E,\phi )} comprising:
Graph theory — ϕ : E → { { x , y } ∣ x , y ∈ V and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle \phi :E\to \{\{x,y\}\mid x,y\in V\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\}} , an incidence function mapping every edge to an unordered pair of vertices (that is, an edge is associated with two distinct vertices).
Graph theory — Graphs as defined in the two definitions above cannot have loops, because a loop joining a vertex x {\displaystyle x} to itself is the edge (for an undirected simple graph) or is incident on (for an undirected multigraph) { x , x } = { x } {\displaystyle \{x,x\}=\{x\}} which is not in { { x , y } ∣ x , y ∈ V and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle \{\{x,y\}\mid x,y\in V\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\}} .
Graph theory — For undirected simple graphs, the definition of E {\displaystyle E} should be modified to E ⊆ { { x , y } ∣ x , y ∈ V } {\displaystyle E\subseteq \{\{x,y\}\mid x,y\in V\}} .
Graph theory — For undirected multigraphs, the definition of ϕ {\displaystyle \phi } should be modified to ϕ : E → { { x , y } ∣ x , y ∈ V } {\displaystyle \phi :E\to \{\{x,y\}\mid x,y\in V\}} .
Graph theory — To avoid ambiguity, these types of objects may be called undirected simple graph permitting loops and undirected multigraph permitting loops (sometimes also undirected pseudograph), respectively.
Graph theory — V {\displaystyle V} and E {\displaystyle E} are usually taken to be finite, and many of the well-known results are not true (or are rather different) for infinite graphs because many of the arguments fail in the infinite case.
Graph theory — Moreover, V {\displaystyle V} is often assumed to be non-empty, but E {\displaystyle E} is allowed to be the empty set.
Graph theory — The degree or valency of a vertex is the number of edges that are incident to it, where a loop is counted twice.
Graph theory — In an undirected simple graph of order n, the maximum degree of each vertex is n − 1 and the maximum size of the graph is ⁠n(n − 1)/2⁠.
Graph theory — The edges of an undirected simple graph permitting loops G {\displaystyle G} induce a symmetric homogeneous relation ∼ {\displaystyle \sim } on the vertices of G {\displaystyle G} that is called the adjacency relation of G {\displaystyle G} .
Graph theory — Specifically, for each edge ( x , y ) {\displaystyle (x,y)} , its endpoints x {\displaystyle x} and y {\displaystyle y} are said to be adjacent to one another, which is denoted x ∼ y {\displaystyle x\sim y} .
Graph theory — In one restricted but very common sense of the term, a directed graph is an ordered pair G = ( V , E ) {\displaystyle G=(V,E)} comprising:
Graph theory — E ⊆ { ( x , y ) ∣ ( x , y ) ∈ V 2 and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle E\subseteq \left\{(x,y)\mid (x,y)\in V^{2}\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\right\}} , a set of edges (also called directed edges, directed links, directed lines, arrows or arcs) which are ordered pairs of vertices (that is, an edge is associated with two distinct vertices).
Graph theory — In set theory and graph theory, V n {\displaystyle V^{n}} denotes the set of n-tuples of elements of V , {\displaystyle V,} that is, ordered sequences of n {\displaystyle n} elements that are not necessarily distinct.
Graph theory — In the edge ( x , y ) {\displaystyle (x,y)} directed from x {\displaystyle x} to y {\displaystyle y} , the vertices x {\displaystyle x} and y {\displaystyle y} are called the endpoints of the edge, x {\displaystyle x} the tail of the edge and y {\displaystyle y} the head of the edge.
Graph theory — The edge ( y , x ) {\displaystyle (y,x)} is called the inverted edge of ( x , y ) {\displaystyle (x,y)} .
Graph theory — Multiple edges, not allowed under the definition above, are two or more edges with both the same tail and the same head.
Graph theory — In one more general sense of the term allowing multiple edges, a directed graph is an ordered triple G = ( V , E , ϕ ) {\displaystyle G=(V,E,\phi )} comprising:
Graph theory — E {\displaystyle E} , a set of edges (also called directed edges, directed links, directed lines, arrows or arcs);
Graph theory — ϕ : E → { ( x , y ) ∣ ( x , y ) ∈ V 2 and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle \phi :E\to \left\{(x,y)\mid (x,y)\in V^{2}\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\right\}} , an incidence function mapping every edge to an ordered pair of vertices (that is, an edge is associated with two distinct vertices).
Graph theory — Directed graphs as defined in the two definitions above cannot have loops, because a loop joining a vertex x {\displaystyle x} to itself is the edge (for a directed simple graph) or is incident on (for a directed multigraph) ( x , x ) {\displaystyle (x,x)} which is not in { ( x , y ) ∣ ( x , y ) ∈ V 2 and x ≠ y } {\displaystyle \left\{(x,y)\mid (x,y)\in V^{2}\;{\textrm {and}}\;x\neq y\right\}} .
